name: Standard Scramble (Appleton Pass / Boulder Lake approach)
beta: This is a non-technical (Class 3) scramble, not a roped climb. Approach on trail to either Boulder Lake (north of the peak) or Appleton Pass (just southeast of the peak), then leave the trail and scramble cross-country up open, steep terrain to the summit ridge and the 6,017-ft high point; the sub-summit South Appleton lies a third of a mile further south along the same ridge.
overview: Mount Appleton (6,017 ft) is one of two summits on a double-topped ridge in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, rising directly above Appleton Pass on the divide between the Sol Duc River and Boulder Creek (South Fork) drainages in the northern Olympics. Its slightly higher neighbor — an informally named sub-peak known locally as "Cotleton" (South Appleton, 6,100+ ft) — sits just 0.33 mile south across a shared saddle. The summit is a sometimes-exposed jumble of orange-red boulders with sweeping views of Mt. Olympus, the Bailey Range, and the Seven Lakes Basin/Cat Creek Ridge area. The peak was named for Dr. Thomas Joseph Appleton (1863–1942), an early Port Angeles physician.

current.approach: Two approaches reach Appleton Pass, the base for the scramble. The Sol Duc approach is now the practical option: from the Sol Duc Trailhead (about 13 road miles off US-101 via Sol Duc Rd, near Sol Duc Falls), follow the Sol Duc River Trail roughly 4.9 miles upriver, crossing Crystal Creek on a suspension bridge, to the signed Appleton Pass Trail junction, then climb about 2.3 miles and ~2,030 ft through forest and subalpine meadow to Appleton Pass (5,100 ft) — about 7.4 miles and 3,100 ft one-way from the trailhead (trailhead about 1,950 ft to pass 5,100 ft). The alternate Boulder Lake/Elwha approach is now far longer: since Olympic Hot Springs Road washed out and was permanently closed to vehicles beyond Madison Falls, reaching the old Boulder Creek Trailhead adds 8 miles one-way of road walking/biking before another ~7.7 miles of trail (via Boulder Creek Campground and Boulder Lake) to the pass — most parties now use the Sol Duc side. From Appleton Pass, leave the maintained trail and follow a climbers' path north up the ridge crest toward Mount Appleton, working around minor outcrops near the crest, traversing onto the north side across a talus basin near 5,400 ft, then regaining the crest at a rock step near 5,800 ft (marked by a distinct rock horn on its south/left side); pass this on an exposed Class 3 heathery gully/ledge system, then continue up talus and heather to the ~6,000-ft notch below the true summit and on to the top.
approach_variant_names: Sol Duc River Trail to Appleton Pass
Boulder Creek from the Elwha
current.descent: Reverse the ridge route back down to the 6,000-ft notch and Appleton Pass. Dropping into the heather/talus basin on the southeast side of the summit makes a good down-route alternative to the exposed Class 3 "goat ramp" encountered higher on the ridge, avoiding that section's exposure on descent. From the pass, retrace the Sol Duc (or Boulder Lake) trail back to the trailhead.
current.pro_needs: No technical pro.
bivy: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
current.rope_note: South Ridge scramble via Appleton Pass/Boulder Lake approach (Olympic NP). Involves Class 3 scrambling on chossy sandstone/slate; a narrow ramp bypasses a gendarme on the ridge, and exposure requires concentration in more than one spot. No rope reported, though a short sling/handline at the gendarme bypass would be a reasonable precaution.

name: Southwest Slopes
beta: This is a remoteness-and-navigation objective more than a technical one — the documented 'easiest route' is class 3 (YDS) scrambling with no reported roped climbing, but it sits far off any maintained trail. No other named technical route (rock face, ridge, or couloir line) is documented on this peak; the subsidiary East Peak (8,160+ ft) was reached separately in 1940 by Fred Beckey's party, likely by a similar approach but not confirmed as the same exact line.
overview: Mount Arriva (8,215 ft) is a long, broken summit ridge at the east end of the Ragged Ridge group in North Cascades National Park, about 1.6 mi southwest of Easy Pass — though it stays hidden from both the pass and SR-20 despite that proximity. The ridge has two high points: East Peak (~8,160+ ft), first climbed by Fred Beckey, Jim Crooks, and Ed Kennedy in August 1940, and the higher true (west) summit, first reached July 6, 1966 by Joe and Joan Firey with John and Irene Meulemans. There is no trail to the peak — parties approach off-trail through Fisher Creek Basin and the Silent Lakes basin, then climb class 3 (occasionally class 4, depending on the exact line) rock on Arriva's south/southwest ridge and ledge systems to the summit. It's commonly combined with nearby Fisher Peak, Kitling Peak, or Graybeard Peak as a multi-day trip.

current.approach: There is no trail to Mount Arriva itself; the standard approach is a 2-3 day off-trail trip via Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes. From the Easy Pass Trailhead (3,700 ft, SR-20 between mileposts 151 and 152), hike the Easy Pass Trail 3.5-3.6 mi and about 2,800 ft to Easy Pass (~6,500 ft), then descend the west side into Fisher Creek Basin. Near the Fisher Camp junction, a boot path heads east/up-valley but fades after about ten minutes at a pile of avalanche-downed trees; from there travel is cross-country up through meadows to the head of Fisher Creek (~6,000 ft — Fisher Overlook Camp is a good base if short on time). From the head of the valley, climb the roughly 1,000-ft headwall to Silent Lakes (~7,000 ft) via either the obvious snow/ice couloir (steeper than it looks, and melts into a loose rock gully by late season) or the broken heather/cliff ramps to its left; ice axe and crampons are useful here into mid-summer. From a camp at Upper Silent Lake, a roughly 1-mile westerly traverse across heather leads to a 7,200-ft saddle, then a rising traverse across a talus bowl gains a key 7,800-ft notch on Arriva's south ridge for the final scramble to the summit.
approach_variant_names: Easy Pass, Fisher Creek Basin and Silent Lakes
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line down the south/southwest ridge and gully/ledge system back to the ~7,800-ft notch and 7,200-ft saddle above Silent Lakes. The rock is loose in places — one trip report documents a 'surfboard-size' rock dislodged by a descending climber that narrowly missed party members below, so descend one at a time and stay out of the fall line. If descending via the Silent Lakes headwall couloir, expect firm snow/ice early season and a loose rock gully late season; many parties prefer the broken heather/cliff ramps just left of the couloir instead.
current.pro_needs: Generally an unroped class 3 scramble; rope optional for the exposed summit area.
current.rope_note: No route-specific beta found. Class 3 hands-on scrambling; standard WA norm is unroped travel, with a light 30m rope occasionally carried by less-experienced parties for confidence on short exposed steps.

name: Boulder Glacier
beta: From high camp on Boulder Ridge (about 5,500-5,900 ft), traverse slightly west-southwest onto the Boulder Glacier and climb the glacier itself, south of and below the Boulder-Park Cleaver, rather than the cleaver. Gain the first 500-1,000 ft working around small crevasses, bear north around a small rock buttress, then head west straight up the glacier; crevasses are the main obstacle on this line and grow more broken through the summer. Above about 9,200 ft the glacier line and the cleaver line merge. Near 9,500 ft, traverse south-southwest about a quarter mile to get around the big rock buttress, watching for rockfall and crevasses, then deal with the bergschrund near 9,800 ft, whose crossing changes through the season. Keep angling west and up to stay clear of the rock band directly below Grant Peak, and finish up a steep snow slope, about the last 500 ft, to the summit plateau beside Grant Peak.
overview: A remote glacier route up Baker's east side that climbs the Boulder Glacier itself: a moderate glacier climb of about 5,200 ft from high camp, with crevasses to thread and a bergschrund to cross. It shares its trailhead, approach and upper mountain with the Boulder-Park Cleaver, which runs up the rib on the glacier's north edge and is the line most parties now choose because it avoids the most crevassed part of the glacier. The arduous, unmaintained approach keeps crowds well below the Coleman-Deming or Easton Glacier routes.

current.approach: From Sedro-Woolley, drive SR 20 east 16 miles to milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Highway (FR 11) for about 18 miles, then (after Boulder Creek Campground) turn onto FR 1130 for about 1 mile to FR 1131, and follow it to the Boulder Ridge Trailhead. Hike the Boulder Ridge Trail (maintained about 2 miles to the wilderness boundary), then a steep, unmaintained boot path with a 3rd-class rock band around 3.4 mi/4,700 ft, continuing up the moraine to high camp on the ridge, roughly 5,500-5,900 ft depending on the snowline, just below the Boulder Glacier.
approach_variant_names: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 to the moraine, then the lower Boulder Glacier
current.descent: Reverse the route: from the summit plateau go back down the Boulder Glacier past the crevasses on the upper glacier, whose bridges soften in the afternoon, and down the cleaver to the high camp on Boulder Ridge (about 5,700 ft, or a flat spot near 7,500 ft under the cleaver). Near the base of the ridge a short steep step, often protected with a fixed line, is downclimbed or rappelled. From camp, follow the steep unmaintained boot path down the heather and the rock band to the Boulder Ridge Trail and out to the trailhead; allow roughly 4 to 5 hours from camp to the car. Descending toward Schriebers Meadow instead ends at a different trailhead on the south side and needs a vehicle waiting there.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier rope, one snow picket per person, and standard crevasse-rescue gear; helmets are strongly recommended for the rockfall-prone traverse below the 9,300 ft buttress.
current.pro_needs: Glacier kit; pickets for the steeper snow

name: Boulder–Park Cleaver
beta: The route follows the Boulder Ridge Trail to its end, then climbs steep heather and a short class 3 rock step onto the ridge, reaching a high camp around 5,700 ft. From there it crosses the lower Boulder Glacier northwest to the base of the cleaver (~6,800 ft), following the cleaver as the climbing steepens, becomes icy, and grows exposed to rockfall near crevasses, before joining the upper mountain near the Boulder Glacier's summit approach.
overview: An east-side route climbing the rock/snow cleaver dividing the Boulder and Park Glaciers — more strenuous and remote than the standard routes but not technically difficult, with the lowest trailhead (2,700 ft) and among the largest elevation gains of any Baker route.

current.approach: Drive Baker Lake Highway to FR1130, then FR1131 to its end at the Boulder Ridge Trailhead (~2,700 ft). Hike the Boulder Ridge Trail #605 — nearly flat through an old clear-cut and timber for about 2 miles to a boggy clearing at the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary — then continue on a rougher user path up steep heather, including a class 3 rock step often protected with a fixed line, to a campsite around 5,700 ft where the ridge meets snow and ice.
approach_variant_names: Boulder Ridge Trail #605 to ridge camp, then across the lower Boulder Glacier to the toe of the cleaver
current.descent: Reverse the cleaver and the lower Boulder Glacier crossing back to the 5,700 ft camp, downclimbing the class 3 step where the fixed line was left, then follow the Boulder Ridge Trail back to the trailhead; expect rockfall exposure near the 9,300 ft buttress on the way down as well as up.
current.detailed_rack: 30m glacier rope (1 per team), 1 picket per person for belays, and for crevasse rescue 4-6 pickets, 1 ice screw, slings and carabiners.
current.pro_needs: Glacier rope team dynamics, crevasse rescue setup, route-finding skills for mid-route navigation

name: Cockscomb Ridge
beta: Grade: 4th class YDS, AI2-3 ice, M1b mixed, PG-13. Technical: 3,000 ft vertical gain over 5 pitches on the ridge itself. Hazards: Extremely loose and unstable rock (especially late season), bergschrunds, extensive crevassing, icefall terrain. Route: From the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, cross Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers northeastward, climb low-moderate snow ramps to ridge at ~7,500 ft, bypass Cockscomb Tower on left via steep snow, continue ridge to summit. Descent: Coleman-Deming Route (easy-moderate glacier). Required: Ice climbing competency, crevasse rescue skills, glacier travel experience, rock scrambling ability. Protection: Few ice screws/pickets, glacier gear essential. Best season: Spring or early summer (late season loose rock creates high hazard). First ascent: July 4, 1961 (Murley, Musser, Vielbig).
overview: Cockscomb Ridge is the true north ridge of Mount Baker — a long, prominent rock-and-ice ridge forming a skyline on the north side of the peak, distinct from the popular 'North Ridge' route (which is actually the NW spur). It sits between the North Ridge and the Park Glacier Headwall and is approached from the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead across the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers. First climbed in its entirety on July 4, 1961 by Chuck Murley, John Musser, and a third climber, after a 1906 Mazama party had been turned back by the ridge's 300-ft Cockscomb Tower.

current.approach: From the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,700 ft) at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39), follow Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles and take the right-hand climbers' path up the Hogsback moraine to camp near 6,000 ft at the edge of the Coleman Glacier. From camp, rope up and cross the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier heading northeast — roughly 2-3 hours of crevassed travel — and take low-to-moderate snow ramps to the foot of the ridge at about 7,500-7,800 ft. Thin snow bridges over a crevasse maze are the main hazard on this crossing.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge, the Hogsback and the Coleman-Roosevelt crossing
Artist Point and Ptarmigan Ridge to the Park Glacier
current.descent: Descend the Coleman-Deming route: cross the summit plateau, go down the Roman Wall to the saddle below Colfax Peak, and follow the Coleman Glacier back to the Hogsback camp, then walk out the Heliotrope Ridge trail to the car.
current.detailed_rack: A few ice screws and pickets plus standard glacier/crevasse-rescue kit; a light rock rack for the loose ridge crest.
current.pro_needs: Pickets and a light rack for the mixed ridge
bivy: Park Glacier camp near the Portals

name: Coleman–Deming Glacier
beta: From Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead, hike through forest and meadow to the Hogsback moraine, then rope up and cross the lower Coleman Glacier, navigating crevasses and seracs, before climbing the Roman Wall (the route's steepest section) and crossing the flat summit plateau to the true summit.
overview: The Coleman–Deming is Mount Baker's most popular route and a classic introduction to glacier mountaineering — a moderate, non-technical climb up two of the peak's big glaciers, finishing with the steeper Roman Wall snow slope to the summit plateau. Heavily glaciated and very scenic, it's the route most guided parties and first-time volcano climbers take.

current.approach: Coleman-Deming on Mount Baker starts at Heliotrope Ridge TH (about 3,700 ft) via Glacier Creek Road (FS 39). Gain about 2,300 ft over roughly 3 miles through forest and alpine meadows, crossing Grouse, Kulshan, and Heliotrope Creeks to reach Hogsback Camp (6,000 ft). Cross creeks in early morning before afternoon glacial melt surge. From Hogsback, rope up on Coleman and Deming Glaciers (crevasses, route-finding). Roman Wall (~40°) is the crux—steep snow between Deming Glacier and summit plateau. Most parties summit on day two.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge Trail #677 to the Hogsback
current.descent: This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent - reverse the ascent line. From the summit plateau, descend the Roman Wall carefully (many parties down-climb facing in on the steepest section, especially if icy or in a whiteout), back onto the Deming Glacier, across the Baker-Colfax saddle, and back down the Coleman Glacier icefall to the Hogsback and high camp. Route-finding through the Coleman icefall's crevasse maze is often trickier on descent (softer afternoon snow, sun-cupped and collapsing snow bridges); parties note snowbridges on this stretch have collapsed in late season and required an end-run around crevasses on climbers' left. No technical rappels are used on the standard route in normal conditions - this is graded a basic glacier mountaineering line. From Hogsback, retrace the Heliotrope Ridge Trail back to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier rope team: 30–40 m rope, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks, pulleys), 1–2 ice screws late season. Locking biners per person.
current.pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for the Roman Wall and running belays through crevasse zones.

name: Coleman Headwall
beta: From a Coleman Glacier camp, climb a lower section of firm steep snow (up to 50°) onto an upper 800-foot band of ~60° ice, crossing two bergschrunds along the way; conditions and exact line vary by year and can involve up to a dozen or more short ice pitches.
overview: A sustained Grade IV ice route up the broken Coleman Glacier's northwest headwall, and one of the more technically complex routes regularly climbed on Baker. From a high camp near 6,600-7,000 ft, the route crosses the broken lower Coleman Glacier to the base of the headwall around 8,500 ft, then climbs roughly 10-14 pitches of sustained 45-50 degree snow/ice with several short steeper steps (occasionally 60-80 degrees) and a crux bergschrund passage near 10,000 ft before easing onto the summit plateau. Most parties start well before dawn and take 8-12 hours camp-to-summit.

current.approach: Start from the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,700 ft, reached via Glacier Creek Rd 39, which reopened to vehicles all the way to the trailhead in August 2026 after flood repairs; it has washed out before, so check its status with the Mount Baker Ranger District before you go). Trail 677 climbs through old-growth forest and flower-filled avalanche chutes; watch for a couple of unbridged creek crossings that can be awkward early season or after rain. At roughly 2.25 mi the maintained trail forks — the left fork continues to the Coleman Glacier overlook, the right fork is the climbers' path that drops toward the moraine and begins the real work. Past Kulshan Cabin's former site (~4,800–5,000 ft, last reliable running water before camp), the trail climbs steeply up the crest of the lateral moraine known as the Hogsback. Most parties establish high camp somewhere on or near the Hogsback between about 6,500 and 7,200 ft — either on the ridge itself or on the flat benches toward the Black Buttes/Roman Nose — roughly 3–3.5 mi and ~3,000 ft above the trailhead. Above camp there is no water except what you melt. From camp, rope up for glacier travel and cross the broken lower Coleman Glacier: the line generally trends up toward ~8,000 ft to meet the North Ridge tracks before dropping back down and cutting under the Roman Nose to reach the base of the headwall near 8,500 ft. This glacier crossing is a genuine route-finding crux that changes year to year — it can involve weaving around large crevasses, crossing questionable snow bridges, and occasionally a committing, barely-reversible crevasse jump or a short vertical step to get established at the base. Because the headwall and the Black Buttes shed rock and ice as the day warms, most parties leave camp in the pre-dawn hours (11 p.m.–4:30 a.m. starts are typical) specifically to be on or past the exposed glacier crossing and lower headwall before the sun hits it.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge to a high Hogsback camp
current.descent: Descent is via the standard Coleman-Deming route, not back down the headwall, and it is a non-technical walk/downclimb with no rappelling required. From the summit plateau, drop down the Roman Wall — a ~35-45° snow slope that most parties downclimb or glissade in a boot-ski — to the saddle between the Black Buttes and Baker's summit dome. From there continue down onto the lower Coleman Glacier, roping back up for crevasse hazard, and retrace the ascent line (or a lower, more direct crossing) back to high camp. From camp, walk back out the Hogsback moraine crest and Heliotrope Ridge Trail 677 to the trailhead — allow 3-4 hours from summit to camp and another 1.5-2.5 hours from camp to the car, longer if the road washout adds its extra miles. No trip reports for this route describe fixed rappels on the standard descent; parties instead glissade/downclimb the Roman Wall on foot. The one place technical rope work sometimes appears is on-route, not on descent proper: if the final bergschrund below the summit ice cap can't be climbed or downclimbed cleanly, some parties build a quick picket or ice-screw/v-thread anchor to belay or lower across it — this is a crux-mitigation tactic during the ascent, not part of the standard walk-off. Because the Roman Wall and glacier crossing are on the sunny south/east aspect, get over them before the snow goes soft; the same crevasse and icefall hazards from the approach apply in reverse on the way down.
current.detailed_rack: Typically 3-5 ice screws and 2-4 snow pickets, and a rope for belayed pitches; a light rock rack is not needed.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the steep headwall
bivy: North Ridge glacier bivy, upper Coleman
Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes

name: Easton Glacier
beta: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow trailhead, approach through forest and meadow, then follow the Railroad Grade lateral moraine up to the toe of the Easton Glacier. The glacier itself is moderately angled with one steeper section on the Roman Wall just below the summit plateau.
overview: The Easton Glacier is Baker's standard south-side route and rivals the Coleman–Deming in popularity — a broad, moderate glacier climb approached via the scenic Railroad Grade moraine, finishing on the same Roman Wall to the summit. The gentler approach and excellent camping make it a favorite for first-timers and for spring skiing.

current.approach: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow Trailhead (~3,360 ft, end of FR 13/Sulphur Creek Road), the route follows Park Butte Trail 603. Cross Sulphur Creek on a footbridge/log crossing near the start (can be a ford in high water), then climb through Schriebers Meadow and forest switchbacks to Morovitz Meadows (about 2.25 miles in). For the Easton Glacier route, leave the Park Butte trail here and bear right onto Railroad Grade Trail 603.2, which climbs the crest of a lateral moraine (the 'railroad grade') with the Easton Glacier dropping away on the right. High camp options are at established sites around 5,600 ft (roughly 3.75 miles from the trailhead) or at Sandy Camp, a cluster of rock-walled tent pads at the moraine's end near 5,900-6,000 ft where the maintained trail effectively ends and glacier travel begins. From Sandy Camp, gain the toe of the Easton Glacier, rope up, and ascend the broad glacier, generally staying climbers' right (east) of the major crevasse bands, to the base of the Roman Wall. Hazards: exposed moraine crest can be loose/exposed in wind, Sulphur Creek crossing can be difficult during peak snowmelt, and there is no reliable water source above Morovitz Meadows other than melting snow.
approach_variant_names: Park Butte Trail 603 and the Railroad Grade to Sandy Camp
current.descent: Non-technical walk-off: reverse the ascent line. From the summit plateau, descend the Roman Wall - a sustained 35-45 degree snow/ice slope that is the crux of the whole route and can be quite icy and rockfall-prone late season; many parties face in and plunge-step or down-climb it carefully - then back down the Easton Glacier to Sandy Camp/high camp, generally retracing the up-track and staying right of the major crevasses. From camp, follow Railroad Grade back down to Morovitz Meadows and out Park Butte Trail 603 to the trailhead. No rappels are used on the standard route; this is one of the two easiest ways up Mount Baker and is regularly guided as a walk-up glacier climb.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier rope team: 30–40 m rope, 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit, 1–2 screws late season. Locking biners per person.
current.pro_needs: Glacier protection only — pickets for the Roman Wall and crevasse zones.
bivy: Sandy Camp, top of the Railroad Grade
Railroad Grade and Morovitz Meadow camps

name: North Ridge
beta: From a Coleman Glacier camp, ascend the west slope of the North Ridge, then continue up the ridge as it steepens below an ice wall at about 9,600 ft — the route's crux, offering left, center, or right-side options through the serac band (the right side involves 70-80° ice with semi-hanging belays). Above the ice wall, moderate snow leads to the summit plateau.
overview: The North Ridge of Mount Baker is the peak's premier moderate alpine ice route and a Cascades classic, first climbed by Fred Beckey, Ralph Widrig, and Dick Widrig in August 1948. From the Heliotrope Ridge approach, cross the Coleman Glacier laterally to the base of the ridge, then ascend snow slopes on the ridge's west flank (with crevasse crossings) to the ice cliff that forms the route's crux — 2-6 belayed pitches of 50-85 degree ice depending on the year and line chosen. Above the cliff, moderate snow/ice leads toward the summit cap, which steepens in its last few hundred feet with real exposure over the west face and a possible crevasse crossing near the summit plateau.

current.approach: Shares the Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead (~3,500-3,700 ft) and the same Trail 677 approach as the Coleman-Deming route: switchback through old growth to the Kulshan Cabin site/treeline fork (~2.25 mi), then up the Hogsback moraine to the standard high camp at ~6,000 ft (about 3 mi and 2,300 ft of gain, 4-5 hours for a laden party). From high camp, the North Ridge approach diverges from Coleman-Deming: rope up and cross the Coleman Glacier heading climbers' left (east), navigating crevasses and icefall, to gain the base of the North Ridge proper on the glacier's true right side. The standard start crosses a double bergschrund via a bridge or narrow snow ramp (can be a difficult, exposed step depending on the season) and climbs a broad 40-degree snow gully to the crest of the ridge. Hazards: crevasse and bergschrund crossing is the technical crux of the approach and is season-dependent (can close out entirely by late summer), icefall exposure on the glacier traverse, and the route sees far less traffic than Coleman-Deming so tracks/bridges may be unbroken.
approach_variant_names: Heliotrope Ridge and the Coleman Glacier crossing
current.descent: The North Ridge is climbed as an ascent-only line - parties do not reverse it. From the ridge crest, 2.5 to 6 belayed pitches of 60-85 degree alpine ice (hardest near the bottom, closer to WI2-3, easing higher) lead up past a prominent ice cliff/ice bulge around 9,600 ft, the route's steepest and most technical section, then the angle eases onto the upper ice cap; trend climbers' left (east) through crevasses to reach the true summit. Descent is via the standard Coleman-Deming route: head west/southwest across the broad summit plateau, down the Roman Wall headwall onto the Deming Glacier, across the Baker-Colfax saddle, and down the Coleman Glacier icefall back to the Hogsback and high camp, then out via Heliotrope Ridge Trail 677. No rappels are used on the standard descent in normal conditions - parties describe it as a straightforward (if long) glacier walk-down, roughly a few hours from summit to camp for a team already familiar with the terrain. A full round trip (approach + climb + descent) commonly runs 10-14 hours from high camp on summit day, roughly matching the Coleman-Deming route's overall mileage/gain — the North Ridge's extra difficulty comes from the technical ice pitches themselves, not a longer approach. Note: if a party needs to bail mid-route on the ice pitches themselves (rare, but possible in bad conditions), teams would need to build v-thread or picket anchors to rappel/lower back down the ice section they'd already climbed, since down-climbing 60-85 degree ice is generally worse than retreating via rope - but this is an emergency contingency, not the standard descent.
current.detailed_rack: 5-7 ice screws, a handful of pickets, a rope for the glacier approach, plus gear for 2-6 belayed ice pitches at the crux cliff.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws for the headwall ice pitches, pickets for snow, full crevasse-rescue capability. No rock pro.

name: Park Glacier Headwall
beta: Glacier travel with crevasse rescue below a steep ice headwall. Longest climb of the northern approaches. From Camp Kiser, primitive boot path leads to Park Glacier and climbing terrain. High exposure with extensive glacier and numerous crevasses. 100+ km² of glaciers and permanent snowfields; iciest mountain in Cascade Range.
overview: A steep ice headwall on the northeast side above the Park Glacier, offering one of Baker's most scenic approaches and a quieter, more remote alpine-ice line than the Coleman Headwall or North Ridge, though not quite as continuously steep as either. One common line climbs three 50m ice pitches up the right-hand ridge to its crest and follows it to the summit; an alternative goes directly up the middle of the headwall from a large bergschrund, passing the left edge of a rock band mid-face. Finding a way across the bergschrund below the headwall largely dictates the line chosen on the upper mountain.

current.approach: From the northeast via Chain Lakes Trail to Ptarmigan Ridge. From Artist Point parking, take Chain Lakes Trail (682) to Ptarmigan Ridge Trail (682.1) junction. Continue about 3 miles west along the ridge to Coleman Pinnacle base, then 0.5 miles to Camp Kiser (~6,000 ft).
approach_variant_names: Artist Point, Ptarmigan Ridge and the Portals
current.descent: Reverse the ascent: descend the Park Glacier, recross the Rainbow Glacier to camp near the Portals, then walk back along Ptarmigan Ridge to Artist Point, taking the lower line north of Coleman Pinnacle to avoid regaining height. Going down the Coleman-Deming instead ends at Heliotrope Ridge on the far side of the mountain and needs a car shuttle.
current.detailed_rack: A standard alpine ice rack of screws and pickets for the schrund ramp and the roughly three ~50m ice pitches above it; exact numbers vary by year and conditions.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the steep headwall
bivy: Park Glacier camp near the Portals

name: Squak Glacier
beta: A moderate glacier climb from the same general trailhead area as Easton Glacier but via the Scott Paul Trail and a separate high camp; skirts the rock Prow and traverses toward Sherman Crater rim before finishing on the Easton/Roman Headwall line to the summit.
overview: A quieter, early-season-friendly alternative to the Easton Glacier, climbing steady snow slopes on Mount Baker's south side past Sherman Peak to join the Easton route near the summit.

current.approach: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow trailhead area, take the Scott Paul Trail; around 4,600 ft leave the maintained trail for the climbers' path to Crag View camp (~6,500 ft, about 3.5 mi from the trailhead with roughly 3,300 ft of gain).
approach_variant_names: Scott Paul Trail to Crag View
current.descent: From the summit, descend the upper mountain via the Easton route, then rejoin the Squak Glacier's descent line back past Sherman Peak to Crag View camp and the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier rope and pickets — basic glacier-travel gear, similar to Easton Glacier.
current.pro_needs: Pickets for crevasse-rescue anchoring; no fixed protection.

name: South Slopes
beta: Mount Ballard's south side is a Class 3 scramble from a camp at the old Azurite Mine on Mill Creek. The approach is the hard part: about six miles up Canyon Creek on trail that is washed out in places past Boulder Creek, then roughly five miles on the Mill Creek trail, most of it buried in slide alder and deadfall. Above camp the climb is steep, rocky ground with two cruxes: a band of brush low on the mountain and, higher up, picking the gully that actually leads to the summit block, where a few short steps need hands. The higher of Ballard's two summits is the southern one. The east ridge from the Slate Creek side is a separate, harder line described under its own approach.
overview: Mount Ballard is a remote, double-summit peak sharing a long ridgeline with its higher neighbor Azurite Peak, near the head of Mill Creek and about 2 miles north of Azurite Peak. It ranks 84th on Washington's 100 highest peaks and rises about 4,000 ft above Mill Creek within roughly a mile, giving it dramatic local relief despite being a non-technical scramble. A 2023 precision survey found the true summit lies about 1,100 ft south of, and higher than, the point long mapped/benchmarked as 'Mount Ballard' (8,301 ft), which is actually a lower north sub-summit. There is no maintained trail to the top; all routes leave trail well below the summit to scramble broad talus, heather, and gully terrain.

current.approach: Standard approach: drive Highway 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead near milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass and follow the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail (#755) up Canyon Creek then Mill Creek — about 11 miles (roughly 6 along Canyon Creek, then 5 up Mill Creek) to the site of the defunct Azurite Mine, then a further ~3 increasingly faint, brush-choked miles (slide alder and downed timber are common since the trail has seen little maintenance since the mine closed) to roughly the 14-mile mark, where a boot path continues about 1.5 more miles to Azurite Pass (6,680+ ft). A longer alternate, more often used for combined Azurite-Ballard trips, starts at the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (#480) near River Bend Campground: follow that trail ~8 miles to the PCT, then the PCT south ~1.5 miles to Horse Heaven Camp before joining the Mill Creek Trail to the pass — this option runs closer to 25 miles round trip with about 6,000 ft of elevation gain.
approach_variant_names: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
West Fork Methow and the PCT
current.descent: Descend the same broad south-facing slopes/gully used on the ascent back down to the basin above the Azurite Mine (~6,600 ft); the scree and talus are loose, so downclimb carefully and avoid being directly above other climbers to prevent knocking rock onto them. From the basin, reverse whichever approach was used (Mill Creek Trail, or Mill Creek plus West Fork Methow River Trail/PCT) back to the trailhead — the lower, brush-choked stretch of the Mill Creek Trail is typically as slow going out as coming in.
current.detailed_rack: No rack is needed.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection exists on the route. It is a Class 3 scramble with a few short, exposed steps near the summit block, normally climbed unroped.
current.rope_note: Documented Ballard routes include a 4th-class corner and a 3rd-class summit block section where some parties use a handline; the South Slopes line itself is standard Class 3 talus/heather and normally climbed unroped.

name: Elwha Basin Scramble
beta: There is no maintained trail on Mount Barnes itself. Parties reach it either along the Bailey Range crest from the Sol Duc to a camp near Bear Pass, or via the long Elwha River Trail to a camp in or near Elwha Basin, then leave the trail entirely and travel cross-country up open slopes/heather benches toward the summit ridge, following the class 2 line. No rope or rack is used on the standard line; the challenge is routefinding and the length/remoteness of the approach, not technical difficulty.
overview: Mount Barnes (5,987 ft) stands in the Bailey Range, above the upper Elwha Basin in the interior of Olympic National Park, within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It rises about 3,200 ft above the basin in roughly two miles, between Mount Queets (1.7 mi SW) and Mount Olympus (6.2 mi W). There is no maintained trail to the peak; it is climbed almost exclusively as a side-summit during the multi-day, off-trail Bailey Range Traverse.

current.approach: No maintained trail leads directly to Mount Barnes — it is a cross-country side-trip off the Bailey Range Traverse. Two main approaches: (1) West via Sol Duc Trailhead — Sol Duc River Trail up to Bogachiel Peak/High Divide (filling water at Heart Lake, the last reliable source for miles), then off-trail east along the Bailey Range crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin, and Stephen Peak to Bear Pass — roughly 3-5 days of travel before reaching Barnes. (2) East via the Elwha River Trail — historically from Whiskey Bend Trailhead (about 26 mi one way with ~6,100 ft gain to the trail's end near Elwha Basin/Dodwell-Rixon Pass); since a washout closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at Madison Falls, Whiskey Bend has had no car access, adding an extra 6.2 mi one-way walk or bike from the Madison Falls parking area just to reach the trailhead. From a camp near Bear Pass or a nearby meadow, the final summit push contours scree and lingering snow patches southeast, then curls north on a boot track up a moderate scree slope to the Class 2 summit — a few hours round trip once camp is established.
approach_variant_names: Bailey Range crest to Bear Pass
Up the Elwha to Elwha Basin
current.descent: Reverse the scree/boot-track line back to the Bear Pass-area camp. Parties continuing south toward Mount Queets and the historic Elwha Snowfinger exit should note the 'snowfinger' has largely melted out in recent years and can no longer be relied on as a snow ramp; expect steep scree, crumbly slabs, and an icy 'snow hump' crossing (microspikes recommended), followed by boulder-hopping the Elwha riverbed and a slow, brushy slide-alder bushwhack (locally nicknamed 'the maze') to regain the Elwha Basin route.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard class 2 route.
current.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped scramble; some parties carry a light ice axe for lingering early/late-season snow on the upper slopes.
bivy: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
current.rope_note: No rope and no rack on the standard line: this is an unroped Class 2 scramble up open slopes and heather benches, and what makes it serious is the routefinding and the length and remoteness of the approach rather than the climbing. Carry a helmet, an ice axe early season, and microspikes even in August for the Elwha snow hump and any lingering shaded snow. Gaiters for the brush, and map, compass and a GPS track, because the terrain is unmarked and off-trail. There is no cell coverage, so a satellite communicator or PLB belongs in the kit.

name: Tribute to Richard
beta: Recorded by its first-ascent party only as a new, relatively short route on the East Face of Mt Bigelow, climbed at 5.10c on August 23, 2011. No pitch count, protection details, or topo are available.
overview: A short, moderate free-climbing line (5.10c) established as a new route on Mount Bigelow's East Face in 2011 — a genuine technical alternative to the peak's Class 3 scrambling routes.

current.approach: Drive to the Crater Creek Trailhead (4,750 ft, 48.2205 / -120.26801). From Twisp take SR 20 south 2 miles to the SR 153 junction, then SR 153 south about 12 miles to County Road 1029 and on to CR 1034 (Gold Creek Road). CR 1034 becomes Forest Road 4340 after roughly 5 miles; continue about 1.6 miles further on FR 4340, then turn onto FR 4340-300 (Crater Creek Road) and follow it 4.6 miles to the trailhead. An alternate description of the same drive starts from Carlton: south on SR 153 for 3.5 miles, right on Gold Creek Loop Road 1.6 miles, right on Gold Creek Road 5.0 miles (becomes FR 4340), 1.6 miles more, then left on FR 4340-300 for 4.4 miles. The gravel is washboarded in places — drive it slowly. From the trailhead take Eagle Lakes Trail #431. The first 0.7 mile climbs gently, rounds a bend into an opening with a view up the Eagle Creek valley, then descends slightly to the bridge over Crater Creek. From there the trail climbs at a consistently gentle grade through mature pine into subalpine fir and larch. At roughly 5 miles the trail reaches the Eagle Lakes area and forks: take the right fork toward Upper Eagle Lake (7,115 ft, 48.213553 / -120.346815, about 6.2 trail miles and 2,350–2,430 ft of gain from the car). Upper Eagle Lake has many campsites and a large horse camp, and is the last reliable water. From the lake, the East Face of Bigelow is the wall directly above to the northwest — bear northwest up talus and heather to the base of the golden granite, roughly 0.4–0.5 mile and 900–1,000 ft above the lake. The FA party put the whole approach at about 8 miles and ~3,500 ft from the trailhead to the base, on a good, fast trail. Scout the line from the lake and from the base before racking up; the crack systems are genuinely hard to read from below.
current.descent: There is no rappel descent and no need for one. From the top of pitch 4 you are standing on the summit ridge; coil the ropes, stow the rack, and walk north a short distance to the true 8,449 ft summit. To get down, retrace the standard scramble line: from the summit, drop southeast and then east down the slopes and gullies that stay right (south) of the prominent rock wall you just climbed — do not try to downclimb into the top of the East Face. The scramble down is Class 2 with a couple of Class 3 moves and about 1,330 ft of loss to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,115 ft. Trend toward the lake basin rather than cutting straight down; the terrain immediately below the wall is broken and steep. Once at the lake, rejoin Eagle Lakes Trail #431 and follow it back down past the Eagle Lakes junction, over the Crater Creek bridge, and out to the Crater Creek Trailhead — roughly 6 miles of very good, fast trail. If you are benighted, Upper Eagle Lake has plentiful established campsites and water and is a far better place to sit out the dark than the loose ground under the face. In an early- or late-season attempt with snow on the slopes, the descent to the lake is the crux of the day rather than the climb — carry an axe.
current.detailed_rack: A double rack to 3 inches is what the first-ascent party carried and what they recommended. They also brought a #4 and used it twice but noted it was not really necessary for the line they chose, and they placed very little small gear — so weight the rack toward hands, fists and off-hands rather than micro-cams and small nuts. Doubles of cams from about 0.5 to #3 covers the fist bulge on pitch 2, the S-crack on pitch 3, and the double fist-and-wider cracks above the crux, where the FA leader ran out of gear and had to traverse off onto face holds to find a stance. A single set of nuts is worth having for the corner and dihedral on pitch 2. A single 60 m rope suffices — the longest pitch is 35 m — and doubles as a rappel line for retreat, though you will leave gear if you use it. Bring a nut tool.
current.pro_needs: Protection is all natural on a crack line with no fixed gear, no bolts and no fixed anchors reported. Placements are good where the cracks are clean but frequently need excavating first, so factor cleaning time into every placement. The wide double cracks above the pitch-3 crux are the section most likely to leave you short — a party that has spent its #2s and #3s low will be running it out there. Belays are on gear at natural stances: an alcove at the base of the fist bulge, a small ledge beside a triangular perched block, and a stance next to a small tower on the summit ridge. Be deliberate about anchor blocks on a lichenous, lightly travelled face; test everything.

name: South Ridge / Southeast Slopes
beta: From the Baker River Trailhead, cross the Baker River suspension bridge and leave the maintained trail near Blum Creek to pick up a faint, flagged climbers' path through dense valley brush and forest, gaining the crest of a rib around 3,300 ft and following it up to the Blum Lakes basin at treeline. From the lakes, climbers traverse counter-clockwise around the upper lake, ascend a steep snow gully/couloir into a snow bowl below the south ridge, cross scree, and follow class 3 (with an exposed class 4 bypass some parties encounter near a notch) blocky ridge terrain to the broad summit plateau. A grassy ledge trending right from the upper snowfield toward the southwest ridge is reported as one of the easier finishes; parties who stray onto the exposed east face have hit sustained class 4 terrain.
overview: Mount Blum (7,685 ft) is a rugged, glacier-draped granite peak on the western edge of North Cascades National Park, the highest of a chain of remote summits strung between Mount Shuksan and the Picket Range. It's named for John Blum, a U.S. Forest Service fire-patrol pilot who died in a 1931 plane crash near Snoqualmie Pass. Two small glaciers cling to its north flank, and the scenic chain of six tarns known as the Blum Lakes sits in cirques on its southeast side. Despite topping out at a modest Class 3 crux, Mount Blum is rarely climbed because the approach is an unmaintained, brutally steep ~9-mile, ~7,000 ft bushwhack with no trail beyond the Baker River crossing — most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip rather than a day climb.

current.approach: Drive Baker Lake Road (Forest Road 11) 25.5 miles north from WA-20 (milepost 82, near Concrete) to its end at the Baker River Trailhead (774 ft; Northwest Forest Pass required, vault toilet on site). Hike the maintained Baker River Trail (#606) roughly 0.5 mile to the Baker River suspension bridge (about 10 minutes). Cross the bridge, then look for a faint, unmarked climber's path beginning about 175 yards downstream of the bridge (and ~25 yards upstream of a stringer bridge) that follows Blum Creek's north bank. The path climbs steeply and indistinctly through dense forest and understory, becoming more defined higher up as it follows Blum Creek Ridge; around 5,100 ft it contours the ridge's south side through huckleberry brush and talus. This climber's path leads to the Blum Lakes basin (roughly 5,000–5,700 ft), roughly 4-4.5 miles and 4,000-4,300 ft of gain from the trailhead to reach the Blum Lakes basin (~5 hours for a fit party); the full round trip to the summit and back is about 9 miles and 7,000 ft.
approach_variant_names: Baker River Trail to the suspension bridge, then the unmarked Blum Creek climbers' path to the Blum Lakes basin
current.descent: Reverse the ascent: down-climb the blocky south ridge/east-ridge terrain into the upper bowl, then retrace the sandy gully back to the upper Blum Lake and around the shoreline to the Middle Blum Lake campsite (roughly 1.5-2 hrs from summit). From camp, re-descend the unmarked climber's path along Blum Creek's north bank to the Baker River Trail and trailhead (about 3 hours).
current.detailed_rack: Not a technical rock route for most parties — no fixed rack is standard. A handful of parties carry a short rope and a few slings/light rack for the class 3-4 notch/bypass or the exposed east-face terrain some climbers inadvertently encounter.
current.pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is typical; the route is graded as a scramble. Parties uncomfortable with exposed, unroped class 3-4 rock near the summit ridge should carry a rope and a small rack (a few slings, cams to ~2in) for a short belayed section.
bivy: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
current.rope_note: South Ridge is Class 3 gully/heather scrambling with a snow couloir leading to a non-technical final ridge, but parties describe roping up for a Class 3-4 rock step near the summit. Carry ice axe for the couloir; a 30m rope with a small rack is a reasonable option for the summit rock.

name: Buckindy Glacier/Scramble Route
beta: The standard (and only non-technical) line on Buckindy climbs class 4 terrain on the north slopes, close by glacier remnants on the mountain's north and east flanks. There is no maintained trail to the peak itself — parties reach it via a multi-day, largely cross-country ridge traverse, most commonly starting from the Green Mountain Trailhead to the south via Suiattle River Road, or alternatively via the Kindy Ridge climbers' trail off Cascade River Road to the north, following the connecting ridgeline of the Buckindy Range. Separate class 5 rock climbing exists on the southwest-facing 'Buckindy Crags,' outside the scope of this standard scramble route.
overview: Mount Buckindy (7,320 ft) is the second-highest summit of the remote Buckindy Range (Buckindy Ridge), a cluster of glaciated, rust-orange-tinted peaks between the Cascade River and Suiattle River drainages, about 20 miles east-northeast of Darrington and southeast of Marblemount, WA. The range's high point is neighboring Mount Misch (7,435 ft); other nearby summits include Sentinel Peak, Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak, and Le Conte Mountain. Buckindy's summit block gets its distinctive rusty color from a mineralized breccia pipe. The peak lies within the Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) land, with small glaciers (Kindy and Goat Creek) on its north and east flanks. It is one of the most rarely climbed summits in the North Cascades — reaching it requires a long, notoriously brutal bushwhack up the Kindy Creek drainage, so most parties encounter it only as part of a multi-day Buckindy Range traverse rather than a standalone day climb.

current.approach: From Darrington, drive north on SR 530 roughly 7-8 miles and turn right onto the Suiattle River Road (FR 26) just after crossing the Sauk River bridge. Follow FR 26 (pavement then gravel) about 20 miles, turn left onto FR 2680, and continue 6 miles to the Green Mountain Trailhead (~3,200 ft). Hike Green Mountain Trail #782 (about 4 miles, ~3,000 ft gain) through old growth and subalpine meadows to the lookout area, then go cross-country along the connecting ridge system east and southeast past the Horse Lake saddle, with slow sidehill travel toward Misch, to Buckindy's north slopes and glacier remnants. This way in is long at present: FR 26 is closed to motor vehicles from milepost 12, about 8 miles below the Green Mountain Road (FR 2680) turnoff, which leaves the trailhead roughly fourteen miles of road past the gate. Check with the Darrington Ranger District before counting on it. The way in that is open comes from the north. Drive Cascade River Road about 14 miles east of Marblemount to Kindy Creek Road (FR 1570), then about 2 miles up that rough spur to a small pullout near 1,850 ft. A climbers' trail climbs Kindy Ridge to a saddle near 4,800 ft south of Point 5116, the same start as for Snowking Mountain. From there, continue south through the Buckindy Range high country to the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages, where parties camp below Buckindy's north side. That ground is a second or third night out.
approach_variant_names: Kindy Ridge from the Kindy Creek road
Green Mountain trail and the Horse Lake saddle
current.descent: Reverse the ascent: downclimb the Class 4 summit block back onto the glacier, stay roped through the crevassed sections of the Kindy/Goat Creek Glacier, then drop back into the cirque and retrace the approach down Kindy Creek to the FR-1570 pullout off Cascade River Road. Buckindy is also approached from the south over Green Mountain from FR 2680, but that road can be reached only past the milepost 12 vehicle closure on FR 26; parties who come in that way exit that way. The two trailheads are in different drainages roughly 70 road miles apart, so pick one and return to it.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard class 4 line. A rope with minimal crevasse-rescue hardware (pickets and/or a couple of screws depending on conditions) for the glacier remnants on the north/east flanks.
current.pro_needs: Glacier-travel protection (pickets, occasional screws) is the main consideration rather than rock protection; the class 4 rock is typically climbed unroped by parties comfortable with sustained exposed scrambling.
bivy: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass

name: Standard Route (Southeast Slopes)
beta: Mount Cameron is a remote, triple-summited peak well off any maintained trail. The standard way up is a long, mostly-easy ridge scramble gained from Cameron Pass via the Grand Pass/Badger Valley trail system out of Obstruction Point (or, on a longer approach, via Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail). From the pass, climbers leave the trail and follow the broad ridge, crossing numerous false summits on mostly Class 1-2 terrain to the true summit; the Class 3-4 spots come only for parties who continue the traverse along the crest to Cameron's other tops. Remnant patches of the Cameron Glaciers and old snow can linger on the ridge's north side into mid-summer.
overview: Mount Cameron is a broad, triple-summited interior Olympic peak (West, Middle, and East tops) in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness, about 21 miles southwest of Sequim. It sits at the head of Cameron Basin/Cameron Pass, between the Grand Valley/Grand Pass drainage to the north and the Dosewallips River canyon to the south, and is named for Amos Benson Cameron, an 1890s homesteader who cut the original trail into the basin. There is no short approach: parties typically reach it either from Obstruction Point via Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail (the shorter, more common option), or up the Dosewallips valley from the south (much longer since a 2002 road washout closed vehicle access). Small remnant snowfields (the Cameron Glaciers) cling to the north side of the mountain well into summer.

current.approach: Primary approach: drive the narrow, one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road (Olympic NP's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft; usually open only early/mid-July through mid-October) 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass, then continue on the Cameron Pass Trail about 3.5 more miles, climbing to Cameron Pass (~6,450-6,500 ft) and the camp sites in the basin below it (roughly 9-10 miles one-way to a base camp, off-trail beyond that to the summit ridge). Alternative southern approach: from Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles since 2002 at a washout about a mile past the road-end parking, some 8.5 miles from US-101, forcing a long walk/bike up the old roadbed before even reaching the Dosewallips River Trail proper and then the multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin — this route adds many extra miles and is rarely used as the primary option today. From Cameron Pass it is about 1.5 miles east along the ridge, with the scrambling mostly in the last half mile (mid July).
approach_variant_names: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail
Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line back down to the Cameron Basin/Cameron Pass camp, then retrace the Cameron Pass Trail and Grand Pass Trail back to the Obstruction Point trailhead (or continue the much longer exit down the Dosewallips if that was the approach used). No rope work or rappels are typical on the standard scramble; the main descent hazards are loose scree/talus on the upper slopes and, early in the season, glissading or downclimbing residual snowfields on north-facing terrain. Dropping straight off the ridge toward Lost Peak in September ran into cliff bands and fourth-class ground; go back along the ridge instead.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: None for the standard line

name: Challenger Glacier
beta: Access via Hannegan Pass or Big Beaver Creek trailheads with multi-day approach through remote wilderness. The route gains the glacier via Easy Ridge or Wiley Ridge, then traverses moderate snowfields, crosses a bergschrund, and finishes with a Class 5 rock pitch on the summit horn. Fixed anchors exist for protection and rappels. The route sees relatively stable conditions July through early September; later season snowbridge degradation can make the bergshrund impassable.
overview: Mount Challenger is the northern anchor of the Picket Range, one of the most remote and rugged sub-ranges in North Cascades National Park. The peak has five summits/highpoints strung along its crest, with the true (highest) summit on the eastern end. Its defining feature is the Challenger Glacier — the largest glacier in the Pickets — which drapes the peak's north/northwest flanks and gives the standard route its name. Because there's no nearby road access, reaching the mountain requires 2-3 days of approach (via Hannegan/Whatcom Pass or via Ross Lake and Wiley Ridge) before any technical climbing begins, making this as much a wilderness expedition as a climb.

current.approach: Two approaches are in common use, both starting from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FS Road 32/Ruth Creek Rd off WA-542). Hannegan Pass Trail #674 climbs a well-graded ~2,000 ft over 4 miles to Hannegan Pass (5,100 ft), the last reliable easy water and the split point for both options. Route A - Whatcom Pass: from the pass, descend a steep, deceptively long ~2,500 ft into the Chilliwack River valley (Boundary Camp), ford the Chilliwack River (log crossings here are unreliable and have caught out parties who lost the crossing and had to bushwhack), then follow the Chilliwack River Trail up through Copper Creek Camp (reliable water, pit toilet, ~7.5 mi from the trailhead) and on to Whatcom Pass backcountry camp (NPS permit required), roughly 6-7 miles beyond the river crossing. From Whatcom Pass you must get around Whatcom Peak (7,574 ft) to reach Perfect Pass: the North Ridge direct is loose, extremely exposed, 'a formidable obstacle' and not recommended for most parties; the standard workaround traverses the Whatcom Glacier on Whatcom Peak's east side, which has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses requiring in-and-out crevasse navigation in low-snow years. Route B - Easy Ridge: from the Chilliwack River Trail below Hannegan Pass, ford the Chilliwack again near Easy Ridge (same log-crossing caveat) and climb steeply onto Easy Ridge (site of an old fire lookout), then follow a faint climbers' path along the ridge crest past tarns and slabby sections (mosquito-heavy in season) over Easy Peak to a notch known as 'the Impasse,' continuing cross-country toward Perfect Pass. Round trip via Easy Ridge alone runs about 26 miles; the full car-to-summit distance by either line is roughly 37 miles (matching this route's recorded ~59.5 km distance), so most parties treat this as a 3-5 day trip with camps at Whatcom Pass and/or Perfect Pass. From Perfect Pass (or the Wiley Lake basin), drop onto the Challenger Glacier at about the 7,000-7,200 ft level - the exact entry point shifts year to year with crevasse conditions - cross a bergschrund, and climb steepening snow (a snow arete in late season) toward the base of the summit rocks. A known late-season hazard just below the summit rocks is a moat that has been reported up to ~5 ft wide and occasionally impassable, forcing a detour to find a snow bridge. From Perfect Pass camp itself, getting down onto the glacier can also involve ~200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, depending on melt-out. The final approach to the true summit is a clean 3rd-class scramble to the base of a short (~50 ft), well-protected 5.5-5.7 rock pitch; many parties fix a handline from the summit rappel anchor down to the top of this scramble to manage the exposure on otherwise solid, unbroken rock.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass, Chilliwack River and Whatcom Pass, then around Whatcom Peak to Perfect Pass
Hannegan Pass, then Easy Ridge and the Impasse to Perfect Pass
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line in essentially all cases - this is not a route with an independent descent gully. From the true summit, downclimb or rappel the short 5.5-5.7 summit pitch: a single rappel off the summit block gets a party back to the top of the 3rd-class scramble. A 30m rope is sufficient for this rappel with a few feet to spare (some parties carry a 40m rope for margin, which is more than enough). The anchor is natural/fixed gear, not bolts: 3-4 old but sound pitons plus a fixed cam or sling, backed up or supplemented as parties see fit; check the tat before committing weight since it is exposed alpine hardware, not a maintained sport anchor. Below the rappel, reverse the scramble and handline section back down to the glacier, watching again for the moat just below the summit rocks that can require hunting for a snow bridge. Continue back down the snow arete and across the Challenger Glacier to Perfect Pass, re-crossing the bergschrund passed on the way up; regaining Perfect Pass itself may retrace the ~200 ft of wet class 4 climbing (and possible short rappel across a moat) noted on the approach. From Perfect Pass, reverse whichever approach line was used to get in - either back over/around Whatcom Peak (Whatcom Glacier traverse, watching for bare-ice sections and open crevasses) to Whatcom Pass and out the Chilliwack River Trail and Hannegan Pass, or back along Easy Ridge and down to the Chilliwack River ford and Hannegan Pass - to the trailhead. Some strong parties instead continue over Eiley-Wiley Ridge toward the Wiley Glacier and Beaver Pass as part of a longer Picket Range traverse exiting at Ross Lake, but that is a variant end, not the standard out-and-back descent for this route.
current.detailed_rack: A handful of small cams (~0.3-1 in) and a few stoppers for the short 5.5-5.7 summit pitch, plus standard glacier travel gear (2-3 pickets, crevasse rescue kit, prusiks). Old fixed pitons exist on the summit block but are weathered — don't rely on them alone.
current.pro_needs: Light rock rack for one short pitch (5.5-5.7); the real technical demand is glacier travel gear and crevasse-rescue competence, not the rack.

name: West Route
beta: Classified a 'Basic Alpine' climb, roughly 10 miles round trip with about 4,600 ft of elevation gain from the historic Grade Creek Road trailhead; a detailed account of a camp-based west-ridge/northwest-face variation logged 14 miles and 6,400 ft round trip. The crux is not technical difficulty but the arduous, often overgrown approach; the final few hundred feet to the summit involve a steep snow ramp/gully flanked by rock bands, commonly climbed with an ice axe and crampons in early-to-mid season.
overview: Mount Chaval (7,127 ft) is a craggy, three-summited peak straddling an east-west ridge (East Peak and Middle Peak, each 7,040 ft, plus the true 7,127-ft summit) in the Glacier Peak Wilderness of the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, roughly 15 miles northeast of Darrington in Skagit County. It sits immediately southwest of its taller, more massive neighbor Snowking Mountain (7,433 ft, 2.5 mi NE) and is built from the Late Cretaceous 'Chaval pluton,' a pyroxene-bearing diorite/tonalite. Richard Merritt and Keith and Ruth Rankin made the first ascent on September 20, 1946. Despite over 1,800 ft of prominence and striking relief above the Illabot Creek and Suiattle River drainages, Chaval is one of the least-visited named summits in the North Cascades — not because the final scrambling is hard, but because every approach (the shorter Illabot Creek Road/west-ramp line, or the longer historical Jug Creek/Bluff Lake/Jug Lake route from the Suiattle side) involves miles of pathless old growth, brush, and steep sidehilling before the climbing even starts.

current.approach: The hike-in starts where FR-16 (Illabot Creek Road) reaches the Arrow Creek switchback (~2,220 ft) — this is the trailhead, not a formal one. A boot/fisherman's path leaves the road roughly 20 yards west of the Arrow Creek crossing and follows the south (right) bank of Illabot Creek upstream through old growth; it's reasonably distinct and has occasional flagging at the ambiguous spots, but it is unmaintained and unsigned, so expect some searching. Follow it about a mile, then turn right, uphill, at the first significant side creek. The crossing near the confluence can be an easy boulder-hop by late summer or a genuine wet ford in early season, so check flow before committing (it's the approach's main creek-ford hazard). Once across, angle east and uphill through a belt of slide alder and brush (the worst brush of the day) trending southeast, then climb through a band of cliffs and gullies around 4,000–4,300 ft — this is the route-finding crux of the approach: intermittent cairns/flagging at best, and it's easy to end up in the wrong gully. A GPS track of a prior ascent (or careful use of a described waypoint like Point 4593') is genuinely useful here. The last dependable water is around 4,000 ft, right before the terrain opens up; above that, water is snow-patch dependent into midsummer. From there the route breaks out onto open west-facing slopes below/west of Pt. 4593', and you traverse and climb east to reach the base of Chaval's broad west face, where the ascent line's obvious left-to-right diagonal ramp begins. Figure roughly 2,000–2,500 ft of gain and 2-3 miles from the Arrow Creek trailhead to the base of the ramp, with parties reporting 4-5 hours car-to-ramp; the gullies just below the west face are avalanche terrain and should not be crossed in unstable early-season snow, and steep sidehilling with real exposure starts once you're above treeline.
approach_variant_names: Illabot Creek Road, Arrow Creek switchback and the west slopes
current.descent: Descent is a reversal of the ascent line, not a walk-off in a different direction: downclimb the same diagonal west-face ramp back down to roughly 4,000-4,300 ft, re-enter the gully/cliff-band system, and pick back down through the brush and slide-alder benches to regain Illabot Creek, re-crossing the side creek near the same spot used on the way up before following the fisherman's path back to the Arrow Creek trailhead. There is no cairned or maintained route for most of this, so route-finding is the primary descent hazard — it's easy to drop into the wrong gully in the cliff band, and carrying a GPS breadcrumb of your ascent (or flagging key turns) is standard practice. The heather- and moss-covered rock on the ramp is more hazardous descending than climbing since holds face the wrong way and the exposure reads more obviously on the way down; a short, steep, exposed Class 3 section near the top of the ramp is where a party might reasonably choose to place a hand line, though this is discretionary, not standard practice. This is a Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed anchors, no bolted rappel stations, and no established rappels — crampons are occasionally useful on lingering snow patches, but a rope is not standard.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard West Route scramble. Parties attempting the harder North Ridge alternate (a distinct, separate line, not this route) should bring a light rack of cams and nuts for low-5th-class rock.
rack: Optional hand line/short rope (exposed Class 3 step near the summit)
current.pro_needs: Standard scramble protection only: ice axe and crampons for the snow sections, no fixed rock protection required on the normal west-ridge/west-face line.
current.rope_note: No technical rock rack on this route. What it takes is an ice axe and crampons for the snow ramp and gullies below the summit pyramid, especially early to mid season, a helmet for the loose, moss-covered rock, and poles for the long brushy sidehilling approach. Competent parties climb the whole thing unroped and nothing is rappelled, though less-experienced parties sometimes carry a hand line or short rope for the exposed Class 3 step near the summit. The descent reverses the same ramp, so the hazard on the way down is route-finding in the cliff band rather than the climbing.

name: North Couloir / Christie Glacier
beta: This is a remote, multi-day approach-plus-climb rather than a roadside route. Parties backpack in via the North Fork Quinault River Trail to Low Divide, then continue cross-country past Martins Park to the base of a couloir on Christie's north side. Crampons and axe are used on the couloir to a north-ridge saddle (~5,600 ft), then the route dips down to and ropes up across the Christie Glacier (steep enough in places that parties rope up even without visible crevasses). A high col just left (east) of the true summit has been reported as unexpectedly difficult — a chossy, eroded, sometimes-overhanging short cliff with a rotten, exposed ledge traverse (class 4) — harder than it used to be, with at least one large rockfall changing the crux between recent seasons. Above the col, dense krummholz gives way to the southeast summit ridge for class 2-3 scrambling to the top.
overview: Mount Christie (6,182 ft) is a glaciated, remote summit deep in the Olympic Mountains' interior, sitting on the divide between the Elwha River (north) and Quinault River (south) drainages within Olympic National Park's wilderness core. It was named for James Halbold Christie, leader of the 1889-90 Seattle Press Expedition that made the first non-Native crossing of the range's unexplored interior. The peak carries the Christie Glacier in its north cirque and is one of the range's most isolated named summits -- the standard approach is roughly 30+ miles round trip from the nearest trailhead, so most parties treat it as a 3-5 day wilderness mountaineering objective rather than a day scramble. There is no simple walk-up: every documented line to the summit (North Couloir-Christie Glacier-East Col-Southeast Ridge, plus a reported East Ridge variation approached from Martins Park meadows) involves snow/glacier travel and at least one short section of loose, exposed rock.

current.approach: From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station/trailhead (elev. ~500 ft, at the end of North Fork Quinault River Road/North Shore Road, ~17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault), follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream through a series of named camps: Wolf Bar (~2.5 mi), Halfway House Camp (~4.6-5.1 mi, ~1,100 ft), Elip Creek (~6.5 mi), Trapper Shelter (~8.1 mi, day/emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp (~13.2 mi, can be thigh-deep in high water), and Low Divide/Renegade Camp (~16-16.7 mi), which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide. From Low Divide, head into the Martins Park/Martin Lakes basin (a side trail off the main Skyline Trail) to establish a high camp on Christie's north side; the broad snow-and-rock couloir leading up toward the peak is visible from Lower Martins Park.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend
current.descent: From the summit, retrace the southeast ridge scramble and krummholz section back to the high col. The chossy, poorly-protected Class 4 step above the col is typically rappelled (~30-50 ft) off a sling/cordage anchor on rock rather than down-climbed, since holds are loose and rockfall-prone. Re-rope for the return crossing of the Christie Glacier -- conditions and moat width vary by year and by time of day (softening snow bridges by afternoon), so parties often aim to cross earlier in the day if repeating the crossing on descent. From the glacier's edge, regain the ridge saddle and descend the entry couloir; with good snow cover this can be glissaded with an ice axe for self-arrest, otherwise down-climb carefully as the lower couloir converts to loose rock and scree later in the season. Watch for parties or rockfall triggered from above on the step and couloir.
current.detailed_rack: One rope (30m+) for the team, 2-3 slings/cordage plus a couple of locking carabiners for the rappel/belay anchor.
current.pro_needs: A single rope (glacier travel plus the short rappel) and a handful of slings/cordage for a hasty rock anchor are sufficient -- this is not a crack- or bolt-protected pitch climb, just a short technical step needing a solid improvised anchor.
bivy: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie

name: Standard Route
beta: From Upper Royal Basin, ascend heather/talus to the moraine rim, drop to snowfields and climb to the ~6,900 ft col between Clark and Mount Johnson. From the col, ascend talus to the cliff base and skirt right on a wide, low-angle (Class 2) southwest-facing ledge — exposed-looking but easy. Where the cliffs split into a Y-shaped gully, go straight up to a boulder then right to a notch on the SE ridge (Class 2-3), descend the ridge to an east ledge via a diagonal crack system (Class 3, exposed but solid), follow the ledge north, then climb a loose gully (Class 3) to a dihedral ramp (Class 4, or a Class 3 broken face alternative on the left) and finally a shallow slot through the north face of the summit block (Class 3-4, good holds). Descend by reversing the route with one short rappel off the summit block. Route-finding is the main difficulty; published descriptions are described by multiple parties as sketchy, and several climbers have produced their own route sketches after the fact.
overview: Mount Clark (7,528 ft) is a striking basalt spire in The Needles, the interior sub-range of the Olympic Mountains, and the second-highest summit in The Needles behind neighboring Sweat Spire (7,580 ft, on Mount Johnson, 0.26 mi SW). First climbed August 21, 1940 by George R. Martin and Elvin Johnson (originally called 'Mt. Belvedere'), it was renamed in 1965 to honor Irving M. Clark, a Seattle conservationist instrumental in establishing Olympic National Park. Deep in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness above Royal Basin, Clark requires a full multi-day approach and is climbed almost exclusively by its 'corkscrew route' -- an exposed, route-finding-intensive scramble that wraps south, east, and north around the summit block. Widely rated a T5 scramble (the hardest informal scrambling grade), it involves sustained Class 3 terrain, one committing Class 3-4 exposed downclimb, and typically a short rappel off the summit block. Trip reports consistently note the scrambling on Clark is more sustained and enjoyable than on nearby Mount Deception, though the rock is generally sounder. A separate roped rock route exists on the central South Face up to 5.5, but the corkscrew is the standard route almost everyone uses.

current.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (2,500 ft, Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District), follow the Royal Basin Trail south along the Dungeness River; at about 1 mile the Royal Basin fork splits off (bear right; do not cross the bridge) from the Dungeness River/Constance Pass Trail. Continue past the Royal Creek and Lower Royal Meadow camp areas to Royal Lake at 7.2 mi / 5,100 ft (roughly 2,600 ft of gain), then about 1 more mile and 500 ft into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft), the standard base camp among the meadows and tarns. From camp, leave the trail and climb talus, boulders, and (early season) snow west-northwest over the moraine rim and across the Surprise Basin snowfields to Surprise Col (~6,920 ft), the Clark-Johnson col, to start the corkscrew route. Alternate approach: via the Dungeness River Trail and Constance Pass Trail to Home Lake, then off-trail through Deception Basin and over Royal Pass into upper Royal Basin -- longer, but useful for a loop trip.
approach_variant_names: Royal Basin and Surprise Basin to the Clark–Johnson col
current.descent: Reverse the corkscrew: downclimb the Class 3-4 slot/dihedral on the north face back to the shallow gully, then descend the loose Class 3 gully to the east ledge (a Class 3 alternative on broken rock just climber's-left of the gully avoids some of the worst choss). Regain the east ledge and climb back up through the diagonal crack -- look for the cairn marking its top, since it's easy to walk past where the ledge appears to cliff out. Cross back over the Y-gully notch on the SE ridge and reverse the Class 2 ledge beneath the cliffs to the Clark-Johnson col / Surprise Col. Many parties instead rig a roughly 60-ft rappel off a natural anchor on the summit block to skip the exposed downclimb. From the col, descend talus and scree back into Surprise Basin and down to Upper Royal Basin camp.
current.detailed_rack: No cam or nut rack is needed on the standard scramble, but carry a 30 m rope and a few slings: they rig a hip belay or handline on the exposed downclimb and a natural anchor for the ~60 ft rappel off the summit block.
current.pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is used -- this is a scramble, not a technical rock climb. Carry a 30 m rope and a few slings to rig a hip belay/handline on the exposed downclimb and a natural rappel anchor off the summit block; a cam/nut rack is typically not needed.

name: Standard Route
beta: Claywood has no maintained summit trail. This line starts at Obstruction Point and follows the Grand Pass Trail over Grand Pass, down into Cameron Basin and steeply up over Cameron Pass, then drops into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River below Lost Pass. From Lost Pass (5,570 ft) the route leaves the trail and heads west-southwest over heather benches, talus and loose shale to the 6,836 ft summit. It is often combined with Lost Peak, Mount Fromme or Sentinel Peak from the same camp. The southern way in, a long valley walk up the Dosewallips to Dose Meadows and then the short, very steep path to Lost Pass, reaches the same pass.
overview: Mount Claywood (6,836 ft) sits at the head of the Lost River in Olympic National Park's interior, about 2.4 mi southwest of taller Mount Cameron (7,190 ft) and roughly 15 mi east of Mount Olympus, with Mt. Fromme just 0.58 mi to its southeast. Lt. Joseph P. O'Neil named it "Mount Clay Wood" in 1885 to honor his commanding officer, Col. Henry Clay Wood — this peak marked the deepest northern penetration of O'Neil's 1885 Olympic exploration expedition. Runoff drains north/west into the Elwha River and east via Claywood Lake to the Dosewallips River. There is no maintained trail to the summit; it is reached only by a long cross-country push beyond Cameron Basin, making it one of the more rarely-climbed named peaks in the park's interior.

current.approach: From the Obstruction Point Trailhead (6,150 ft), reached by the narrow, unpaved Obstruction Point Road that leaves Hurricane Ridge Road just below Hurricane Ridge, follow the Grand Pass Trail along open Lillian Ridge, then down into Grand Valley past Grand and Moose Lakes and up past Gladys Lake to Grand Pass (6,488 ft) at about 6 miles.
