Net gain to the pass is only a few hundred feet, but the trail first loses well over 1,000 ft into the valley, so total climbing to the pass is close to 2,000 ft. Beyond Grand Pass the trail drops steeply into Cameron Basin, then climbs steeply to Cameron Pass (6,448 ft), the highest trail-served pass in the park; the last part of that climb is loose and rocky in spots and holds snow into midsummer. From Cameron Pass the primitive trail descends into Lost Basin at the head of the Lost River and continues to Lost Pass (5,570 ft), the low notch between Lost Peak and Claywood. Parties camp in Upper Cameron Basin or in Lost Basin and climb the peak from there. At Lost Pass leave the trail and head west-southwest across open heather benches and talus toward Claywood, the higher, greyer and more broken summit about a mile and a half away. The final several hundred feet are class 2-3 scrambling on broken shale and loose scree, with a short class 3 step on the west side of the summit block. Everything beyond Lost Pass is unmarked and off-trail, so carry a map and GPS and go only in good visibility. Above Lost Pass a workable line climbs steep slopes and light brush to the 6,068 ft bump, then follows a ramp system on the east side of the summit block; it looks too steep from a distance but goes.
approach_variant_names: Dose Meadows and Lost Pass
current.descent: This is a walk-off and downclimb; no rappels are needed. Reverse the class 2-3 scramble carefully on the loose shale, then return east-northeast over the talus and heather benches to Lost Pass and back to camp. To exit, climb out of Lost Basin to Cameron Pass, descend steeply into Cameron Basin, climb back over Grand Pass and follow the Grand Pass Trail through Grand Valley and along Lillian Ridge to Obstruction Point. The loose, steep ground on both sides of Cameron Pass is slower than it looks, and snow can linger there early in the season. Watch for afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge on the final miles. This is a multi-day trip built around a basin camp, not a single day.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock gear for the standard scramble.
current.pro_needs: None for the standard line

name: West Arête
beta: From Crystal Pass (base of the West Arête), begin a rising traverse on the right side of the ridge crest at ~10:30 AM (typical timing). Terrain involves fairly broken Class 2 and 3 with occasional 4th or low 5th steps. Bypass towers via a ledge on the right side. Reach the crux step on the arête proper—traverse up and right on a groove (5.4), clip existing pitons, move straight up (5.4) then back left to a small alcove below a chimney. Anchor and ascend the chimney leftward to a sloping ledge, then traverse left to easier ground. Continue to ridge crest with talus climbing above, then cross to east side following the standard route descent to summit horn.
overview: A more sustained, technical alternative to the standard scramble: roughly 1,100 feet of mostly broken class 3-4 rock with a few low-fifth-class steps over 5+ pitches, the hardest about 5.4-5.5, climbing the arete that rises directly above Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon to the summit ridge. From Crystal Pass, traverse around a small tower to the start; climb a vertical crack protected by fixed webbing, then right-trending class 3 ledges to the arete crest. The route crosses occasionally snowy sections along the crest to a large ledge, then the crux: a right-trending ledge that cuts back left past a couple of fixed pitons into a chimney, followed by short face climbing and a hand traverse (sometimes snow-covered) before easing into scree near the summit ridge. Several belays use fixed pitons or slung anchors left in place.

current.approach: Same trailhead and grueling approach as the standard route: a road-walk/bike of roughly 5 miles up the closed, washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the Lake Constance climbers' trail (~1,450 ft), then a steep, unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles — no switchbacks, hand-over-hand in places — to Lake Constance (4,800 ft); figure 2.5-3.5 hours. Camp at the established sites on the lake's north end. From there, instead of cutting into the South Chute, continue up into Avalanche Canyon past the 'Thumb' rock feature and stay toward the climber's-right side of the canyon passing below the 'Cat Ears' landmark, following a rough path through scree and talus that fades out below the South Chute turnoff. The canyon is roughly 1.5 miles of steady uphill slog to Crystal Pass at its head; this terrain is loose, poorly consolidated talus/scree when snow-free and considerably faster and safer when covered in firm early-season snow (carry an ice axe June into July). The final few hundred feet to Crystal Pass steepen and often hold softening snow by mid-morning, so an early start pays off. Plan roughly 3-4 hours from the lake to the pass.
approach_variant_names: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to Crystal Pass
current.descent: There is no established rappel line down the West Arête itself, and no party descends the way they came up. From the summit, most climbers descend via the Finger Traverse or, conditions permitting, the Terrible Traverse, both of which drop into the South (or North) Chute scree system rather than back down the arête. Expect exposed class 3 ledges and a short stretch of downward-facing scrambling around a blind corner on the Finger Traverse; parties caught in poor visibility or wet snow have specifically reported bypassing the Terrible Traverse in favor of the Finger Traverse for this reason. Below the traverse, descend the South Chute's scree back into Avalanche Canyon, retrace the canyon to Lake Constance, then descend the steep climbers' trail to the road. As with the other Constance lines, the only rappel most parties encounter is an optional short ~20 ft rap off a fixed sling/anchor on the small class 3-4 summit block — many parties downclimb this instead, so it isn't mandatory. no published account gives roped rappelling on the arête route itself or its connecting descent gullies; a single 30-60m rope is more than sufficient for the optional summit-block rap if used. Given the pillow-basalt rock (loose and often runout), a helmet and careful hand-testing matter more on this descent than rope work.
current.detailed_rack: Single light rack to ~2 inches with slings; rope for exposed steps
current.pro_needs: Moderate alpine rock pro; belay the more exposed steps on the arête
bivy: Lake Constance — the standard base for the South Chute

name: Northeast Ridge
beta: Downclimbed from Crowder's summit toward Pickell Pass in 2012, the ridge is a winding line of grassy 3rd class ledges with an occasional 4th class move and one or two short 5th class downclimbing moves — slow, tedious going where a slip is not an option. A several-hundred-foot-long chasm (possibly a fault) cuts across the lower ridge, and the party ultimately had to find a break in a final cliff band and a scree slope to reach Pickell Pass; one partner chose to rappel sections that the other downclimbed.
overview: A direct, technical ridge line dropping northeast off Crowder's summit toward Pickell Pass. It is documented as a descent used by parties continuing a Pickets high-route traverse northward, not as a recommended way to reach Crowder's summit, and is significantly harder and more hazardous than the Southwest Route.

current.approach: Reached only by first climbing Mount Crowder by its Southwest Route, from the col between Phantom Peak and Crowder, and continuing down the far side; there is no separate trailhead approach to this ridge on its own.
current.descent: From the summit, the ridge is down-climbed via a mix of loose, grassy Class 3-4 ledges with occasional low-5th-class moves, working around a large chasm partway down, and negotiating a final cliff band (found via a scree-slope break) before reaching Pickell Pass.
current.pro_needs: At least a short rappel rope/light rack for occasional cliff bands has been used by the one party to document this line; treat it as requiring rope and some protection for short sections, not a pure scramble.

name: Southwest Route
beta: Once through the approach, the SW Flank itself is a moderate 3rd/4th-class scramble on open slopes and ledges to the summit — no technical rock climbing required. Parties doing a standalone ascent typically descend the way they came; parties continuing a larger Pickets traverse instead descend the far more serious NE Ridge toward Pickell Pass.
overview: Mount Crowder (7,082 ft) is a remote summit at the high point of a ridge running south from Phantom Peak in the Picket Range, North Cascades National Park, between upper Goodell Creek and Picket Creek, about 1.7 mi southwest of Mount Fury and just south of its parent peak, Phantom Peak. It has 1,042 ft of prominence and 1.53 mi of isolation. First climbed in 1962 by Cal Magnusson, Jack Ardussi, Don Mech, and Don Schmechel when it was still known informally as 'Old Brownie,' the peak was officially renamed in 1970 by the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to honor Dr. Dwight F. Crowder (1929-1970), a USGS geologist, mountaineer, and North Cascades conservationist credited with several first ascents in the range, including South Spectacle Butte and Sitkum Spire. Crowder sits deep in the trailless heart of the Pickets and is almost never climbed as a standalone objective — nearly all recorded ascents are one summit within a multi-day Picket Range ridge enchainment.

current.approach:
Crowder has no trail and no road anywhere near it, and the way in is from the north, down the west side of the Picket Range. From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead, walk over Hannegan Pass and down to the Chilliwack River, ford it, and climb onto Easy Ridge. Follow the ridge over Easy Peak, get around the Imperfect Impasse gap (in most years by dropping well below it and climbing back up an exposed class 4 step) and carry on to Perfect Pass. From there keep heading south across the western slopes of the range, below Challenger, Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, to the west side of Phantom Peak, then continue south to the col between Phantom and Crowder, at a little over 6,000 ft, where the climb starts. Allow at least two days to reach the col.

The other way in comes from the west and is seldom used: the Baker River Trail, then the high route along Pioneer Ridge, whose southeast end sits at the bottom of Crowder's easy southwest slopes.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Perfect Pass, then south along the west side of the range to the Phantom-Crowder col
Baker River Trail and the Pioneer Ridge high route
current.descent: Descend by reversing the SW Flank exactly as climbed: down the easy 2nd/3rd-class scree and heather ramps to the Phantom–Crowder col, then back north along the west side of the range the way you came. This is a walk-off/downclimb on the standard route — no rappels are required. Do not be tempted to shortcut east off the NE Ridge toward Pickell Pass: a first-hand account found this alternative deceptively difficult — in practice descending it means weaving a convoluted line of grassy 3rd-class ledges broken by short, exposed 4th-class and even a couple of 5th-class downclimbing moves, past a major chasm/fault splitting the lower ridge, with an unprotectable vertical drop near the base that forced one climber in that party to rig an improvised rappel off natural gear (there is no fixed hardware anywhere on this peak) rather than downclimb it. On the standard SW Flank descent, plan on 0 rappels; a rope is not needed for the reversal, just careful 3rd-class scrambling technique and, ideally, a GPS track of your ascent line given the routefinding-heavy terrain.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the SW Flank scramble itself. Parties planning the alternative NE Ridge descent (as part of a larger traverse) commonly carry a light rope and a small rack/slings for the short 4th/5th-class downclimbing and occasional rappel.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock gear — a few slings and small cams/nuts are enough for the occasional short rappel anchor or belayed step; this is a scrambling route, not a pitched rock climb.
bivy: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone

name: Northwest Face/Corner
beta: A 5.7 trad route (multi-grade string '5.7 / 5a / 15 / V+ / 13 / MVS / 4b') with a PG13 hazard rating, indicating some sparse/serious protection; detailed pitch-by-pitch beta has not been published anywhere accessible, unlike the well-recorded South Corner.
overview: A short, sporty pitch (5.7 PG13) on the northwest aspect of Cruiser's summit pinnacle, reached by continuing along the crest of Sawtooth Ridge past the South Corner start. It is a separate, established 1-pitch route alongside the 2-pitch South Corner — the mountain's only two recorded technical lines — rather than merely a variation encountered during a full Sawtooth Ridge traverse. Often combined with, or climbed as an alternate finish to, the South Corner during a visit to the ridge.

current.approach: Same approach as the South Corner (Staircase → Flapjack Lakes → Needle Pass, closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire — see Closures). From Needle Pass, continue along or near the crest of Sawtooth Ridge past the South Corner start line to reach the northwest side of Cruiser's summit pinnacle via exposed 3rd/4th-class ridge scrambling.
current.descent: From the topout, make a short but exposed Class 3 scramble to the true summit, then descend via the standard South Corner bolted double-anchor rappel station and reverse the South Corner descent (Class 4 gully, Cannon Hole tunnel, Needle Pass couloir) back to Flapjack Lakes.
current.detailed_rack: Lots of micro brass placements on sometimes very questionable rock—test every placement, as the rock is friable and a found placement may not hold a fall. Small gear and long slings for the arete.
current.pro_needs: Cryptic, sparse pro requiring careful gear sense on friable rock; this is the PG13 character of the route.
bivy: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out

name: South Corner
beta: From a high camp at Flapjack Lakes (or Mildred Lakes), climbers traverse toward Gladys Divide, ascend a snow/scree gully to Needle Pass, and follow a boot-marked but exposed Class 3 ridge crest north to the base of Mt. Cruiser's south side. A Class 4 gully leads past the cannon-hole chockstone to a platform, and from there a short low-5th-class face pitch, protected by small cams/nuts plus a bolt and reportedly an old piton partway up, reaches a bolted belay on the ridge crest; an easy but very exposed ridge-crest pitch then reaches the true summit. Rock quality is good for the Olympics but protection is sparse and runout in places.
overview: The classic and easiest technical line up Mount Cruiser (6,104 ft), the highest summit on the Olympic Mountains' Sawtooth Ridge and the objective most parties travel to the ridge for. From Needle Pass the route follows a Class 4 gully past a large chockstone ('Cannon Hole,' passed via a short squeeze/tunnel) to a broad, exposed platform. From the platform's end, a low-5th-class face pitch — variously rated 5.0 and 5.3 — leads to a belay on the summit ridge crest, followed by a short, very exposed Class 3 scramble to the true summit.

current.approach: From the Staircase Ranger Station (~770-850 ft, at the end of Lake Cushman Rd/North Fork Skokomish Rd), the approach starts on the North Fork Skokomish River Trail, a gently graded old decommissioned roadbed that runs up-valley through old-growth forest for about 3.7-3.8 miles to the former road-end/Spike Camp junction with the Flapjack Lakes Trail. Bear onto the Flapjack Lakes Trail, which climbs steadily and then steeply (with one rough slide/washout bypass to pick through) for about 4 more miles, gaining about 2,000 ft, to reach Flapjack Lakes (~3,850 ft, about 7.5-8 miles from the trailhead) - the standard base camp. Flapjack Lakes is a designated, permit-limited backcountry camp, so reserve ahead for summer weekends. Reliable water is available at the lakes and at several creek crossings on the lower trail; treat before drinking. From camp, continue about 1.5 miles on maintained trail up-basin toward Gladys Divide; just before the divide, leave the trail and climb southeast up a steep snow/scree couloir (several hundred feet of gain, often 35-40+ degrees) to Needle Pass. This couloir holds firm, icy snow well into summer, and crampons plus an ice axe are advisable for most of the season - it's the single biggest hazard of the approach, since a slip on hard snow here has real consequences. From Needle Pass, turn left (east) and scramble exposed Class 3 terrain to the summit of Beta Peak, descend through its right-most summit notch (one Class 4 move and a short gully), traverse high toward Cruiser, then drop down a longer connecting gully to reach Cruiser's base, where the roped climbing begins (a Class 4 gully leads to a large chockstone; go left around it and squeeze through a short tunnel to reach the platform below the 5.0 pitch). All told this is roughly 8-9 miles from the trailhead to the base of the technical climbing, crossing Needle Pass at about 5,700 ft on the way, typically 5-7 hours to camp and another push to the base the next day. Fog and low cloud are common on the ridge and ridge-basin route-finding above Flapjack Lakes is easy to lose in flat light, so know the boot-tread line before committing.
approach_variant_names: Flapjack Lakes and the Needle Pass couloir
current.descent: Reverse the exposed Class 3 ridge-crest scramble/downclimb back to the top of the technical ground, then begin rappelling. The first rappel drops from a bolted anchor on the ridge crest - parties describe a solid, relatively new 2-bolt station, but also note nearby older rusted 1/4-inch bolts and pitons that should NOT be trusted, so identify the anchor carefully before weighting it - down about 25 meters to a large ledge/platform. From the platform, two more rappels of roughly 30 meters each continue down the Class 4 gully (past the chockstone/tunnel squeeze used on the way up) to reach the base of the route, for three rappels total. A single 60m rope, used doubled, comfortably covers all three rappel distances; a 50m rope has been used but is tight on the longer stretches and some parties add a short bit of roped downclimbing near the top to make it work - bring 60m if you have the choice. From the base of the climb, reverse the connecting gully and the Class 4 step back over Beta Peak's notch to Needle Pass (no further rappelling needed here, just careful downclimbing/scrambling), then downclimb or plunge-step the snow couloir back down to Gladys Divide - soft afternoon snow sometimes allows a short glissade, but the icy, rocky runout makes this a judgment call rather than a given - and walk out via Flapjack Lakes to Staircase.
current.detailed_rack: Full set of small wired nuts, a few cams from finger-size to about 2 in, and a small selection of alpine draws/slings. A couple of fixed bolts exist on the crux pitch and at the rappel anchor but are of mixed age/quality — don't rely on them exclusively.
current.pro_needs: Sparse but adequate: small nuts/cams to about 2 in protect the crux face, supplemented by a bolted anchor at the rappel station (inspect condition first).
bivy: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out

name: Standard Route / South Side
beta: This is the most frequently ascended route. Start from Ouzel Lake (~5,700 ft) and head eastward up the west slopes, which are semi-open initially and transition to alpine terrain around 6,200 ft. Minor cliffbands require Class 3 scrambling to navigate around. Climb to the obvious SW basin (~7,700 ft), continue to the 8,260-ft notch immediately south of the summit, then traverse the final chossy South Ridge to the summit. Descent is more technical than ascent and may require roped sections. The peak is known for exceptionally loose, fractured volcanic rock throughout.
overview: Mount Custer is a high, glaciated summit on the international border ridge near Mount Spickard and Mount Rahm, deep in the remote Chilliwack zone of North Cascades National Park. It's named for Henry Custer, a topographer who surveyed the US-Canada boundary through this area in the 1850s. The peak sits within an old volcanic caldera and is infamous for exceptionally loose, fractured, oxidized volcanic breccia — climbers commonly nickname it "Chosster," and one summit register entry summed up the rock as horrible. Two small glaciers (Custer Glacier, higher, and the larger Maselpanik Glacier lower in the cirque) mantle the north side, but the standard South Side route described here stays on rock, scree, and snow rather than glacier ice. First recorded ascent 1958 (Frank Dawe, Roy Mason, Karl Teichman).

current.approach: From the Depot Creek trailhead (reached via the unsigned dirt spur off Chilliwack Lake Road in BC), follow the old Depot Creek logging-road grade south about 3.2 miles (drivable in part, to a washout) to its end, then about 150 yards of trail through old growth to the border obelisk (Monument 65, about 2,750 ft) and trail register, then continue on the fading Depot Creek path up the valley. The first stretch follows an old roadbed for under a mile before it vanishes into forest; for roughly 3 miles the route weaves through timber and brush with no consistent tread. At the valley's headwall (about 3,800 ft at its base to 4,800 ft at its top) the trail parallels a waterfall on Depot Creek — expect a stream crossing at its base, wet slabs, and at least two fixed/dangling handlines on the exposed slab sections beside the falls (a real fall hazard if wet or icy). Above the falls the path becomes fainter through talus and brush in the open basin below Mount Redoubt before reaching Lake Ouzel (5,700 ft, ~8-9 miles and ~3,500 ft gain from the car, 5-6 hours), the standard base camp on flat sandy benches. From camp, scramble up the large broken buttress southwest of the lake (cairned to aid the return); partway up the buttress traverse far climber's-right, then continue up to gain the Redoubt Glacier easily. Cross/skirt the glacier (crevasse hazard, rope up if conditions warrant) to reach the obvious SW basin near 7,700 ft below Custer's summit, then continue to the 8,260-ft notch immediately south of the true summit. A short, vertical, 6-8-ft-wide rock gully (with occasional ice) breaks through here — this is the technical crux of the ascent.
approach_variant_names: Depot Creek from the Canadian side, Lake Ouzel and the Redoubt Glacier
current.descent: Descend by the same line: the loose South Ridge back down to the 8,260-ft notch, then downclimb the short crux gully (three accounts describe this as a Class 3-4 downclimb; short-rope or a single short rappel off a natural rock/boulder anchor is reasonable if the gully is wet, icy, or a party is uncomfortable downclimbing — trip reports from parties on Custer's south side describe a rap anchor slung around a boulder near a similar snow-gully exit, so treat any rappel here as a natural (sling-around-boulder or horn) anchor, not bolted). Below the notch, retrace the SW basin and Redoubt Glacier crossing, then follow the cairned line down the broken buttress back to Lake Ouzel and camp — cairns were specifically placed to prevent route-finding confusion here, so watch for them, especially in flat light. No fixed/bolted rappel stations exist on this route; treat it as a walk-off/downclimb route with the possibility of one short improvised rappel at the crux gully in bad conditions.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit plus a few small pieces and slings for the short summit rock.
current.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel and snow lead to exposed Class 3-4 scrambling; minimal rock pro needed.

name: Mount Dana Scramble
beta: Mount Dana is a class 2 scramble with no pitch-by-pitch detail published. The line with a described approach leaves the Elwha Basin way trail beyond Happy Hollow, climbs steeply north through brush and timber to the ridge joining Mount Barnes and Mount Wilder, and follows that crest high, past Wilder, to Dana's summit. Treat it as a route-finding, self-sufficient objective rather than a beta-rich one.
overview: Mount Dana (6,213 ft, ~1,529 ft prominence) is an isolated, trailless summit in the Bailey Range, part of Olympic National Park's rugged interior above the headwaters of the Elwha River. It was named by the 1889-90 Seattle Press Expedition — the party that first explored the Olympic interior and named most of the Bailey Range — for Charles A. Dana, an editor of the New York Sun. The first recorded ascent was in 1928 by a USGS survey party. The peak is built of Eocene-age basalt typical of the Olympic core rocks, and its nearest higher neighbor is Mount Norton (6,397 ft), about 3.9 miles away. There is no maintained trail anywhere near the summit; climbers reach it on a multi-day trip up the Elwha, climbing out of the upper valley to the ridge it shares with Mount Wilder, making it one of the more committing sub-6,500-ft summits in the park.

current.approach: Getting to the trailhead is part of the approach: flood damage has closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at the Madison Falls parking area, and that closure adds about 6.2 miles each way of road walking or biking just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road remains open to foot/bike traffic beyond Madison Falls). From Whiskey Bend, the actual hike-in follows the Elwha River Trail, a well-graded historic path along the river's east bank that passes the old Geyser Valley homestead sites (Michael's Cabin, Humes Ranch) in the first mile or two. The trail is mellow by Olympic standards, staying under roughly 2,000 ft of gain through its first 15+ miles, and passes Lillian River junction (~4 mi), Mary's Falls Camp (8.8 mi), Canyon Camp, Elkhorn Guard Station, and Stony Point as it winds upstream through old-growth forest with the Elwha River itself as a constant, reliable water source. Camp Wilder and Hayes River Guard Station mark roughly the trail's halfway point. Continue up the valley to Chicago Camp, roughly 24-26 trail miles from Whiskey Bend, where the Elwha River must be forded; check conditions before you go, since the crossing can be genuinely hazardous in early-season high water or after rain. At Chicago Camp leave the main trail, which turns south for Low Divide, and take the fainter way trail west up the Elwha toward Elwha Basin, past Happy Hollow camp. Beyond Happy Hollow the route leaves all paths: strike north up the valley side, steep and brushy through timber, to the crest of the ridge that joins Mount Barnes and Mount Wilder. There is no path on the ridge either. Stay high and follow the crest east toward Mount Wilder and then northeast to Dana, finishing with a class 2 scramble to the 6,213-ft summit. Water is scarce once you leave the valley floor, so carry enough for a camp on the ridge. This is a trip of several days, and solid off-trail navigation is essential from Chicago Camp on.
current.descent: This is a walk-off and scramble-down; nothing on Mount Dana or its ridge is rappelled. From the summit, reverse the ascent: back southwest along the crest toward Mount Wilder to the point where you topped out on the Barnes–Wilder ridge, then down the steep, brushy slope to the Elwha Basin way trail near Happy Hollow. The brush and timber below the ridge are where parties lose the line on the way down, so note landmarks where you gained the crest before you leave it. From the way trail, walk back down to Chicago Camp, re-ford the Elwha, and follow the Elwha River Trail out to Whiskey Bend, plus the road walk or ride back to Madison Falls while the Olympic Hot Springs Road washout stands. No anchors, fixed or natural, come into play anywhere on this route.
bivy: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
current.rope_note: Little is published about this peak specifically, so treat it as a route-finding, self-sufficient objective rather than a beta-rich one and carry navigation before you carry hardware: map, compass and a GPS track for extensive off-trail travel. Nothing here is rappelled and no rack is needed. An ice axe early season, and crampons if hard snow is sitting on the ridge or in the gullies below it, are what the terrain actually asks for, along with a helmet and footwear you can ford a river in.

name: Standard Scramble (Royal Basin)
beta: Approach via Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Follow Upper Dungeness Trail 1 mile to Royal Basin Trail junction. Continue about 6 more miles to Royal Lake (5,100 ft; 7.2 miles from the trailhead) and 0.8 miles more to Upper Royal Basin (5,600 ft). From Upper Basin camp, climb southwest over glacial moraine ~1 mile to base of northeast face. Ascend steep slope (30-50 degrees) to ridge crest, then follow ridge to summit. Class 2-3 scrambling with extreme loose rock. 5+ hours from camp. Helmet mandatory. Descent reverses route with rockfall watch.
overview: Mount Deception (7,788 ft) is the second-highest summit in the Olympic Mountains after Mount Olympus, and the highest point in the eastern Olympics. It rises at the head of Royal Basin above Royal Creek within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, Jefferson County. The peak is built of notoriously rotten Eocene-age pillow basalt — regarded as some of the loosest rock in Washington — and takes its name from the difficulty early climbers had finding a route through its near-constant cloud cover; it was originally called Mount Holmes by the 1889-90 Seattle Press Expedition. The Standard Route climbs from Upper Royal Basin over a glacial moraine to the low point on the Deception-Martin ridge, crosses the small Deception Glacier remnant, and ascends a ~45-degree snow/rock gully to the saddle beside Gilhooley Tower before easing onto Class 2 slopes for the final push to the summit.

current.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (2,500 ft, end of FR 2870; USFS day-use fee/permit required), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833.2). The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River; at about 1 mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right onto FST 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream. The trail climbs gradually through forest, transitioning to open rocky, brushy terrain above roughly 4,000 ft, then reaches Royal Lake (5,100 ft) at about 6-7 miles from the trailhead (~2,500-2,600 ft gain to this point) — the last reliable, easy water and a common overnight camp for a 2-3 day itinerary. From the lake, circle to its far end and continue past Shelter Rock, a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter, then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet stream into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600-5,700 ft), roughly 1 more mile and 500 ft of gain — another good camp and water source (snowmelt tarns/stream, treat before drinking). From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine (~1 mile) to the base of a large snow (or, late-season, mud/scree) slope on the west edge of Deception's northeast face; this slope leads up toward the Deception-Martin saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Route-finding on the moraine and lower slope is straightforward but the rock throughout the upper mountain is loose, rotten pillow lava — helmet mandatory from here up, and watch for rockfall triggered by parties above. Above the saddle, descend/traverse about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant and work westward around Gilhooley Tower and adjoining crags (go around to the west — do not try to climb over) to reach class 2 slopes leading to the summit; the alternate line through Surprise Basin avoids the steepest ground but is long, arduous, and not recommended.
approach_variant_names: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin to Gilhooley Saddle
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: from the summit, walk the class 2 slopes back around the west side of Gilhooley Tower and the adjoining crags, regain the Deception-Martin saddle area, and descend the same snow/mud/scree slope back onto the upper moraine and into Upper Royal Basin. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble descent with no rappelling required anywhere on the standard route — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rap stations are reported on this line. The steep upper slope is the crux of the descent: several parties describe it as loose rock, hard mud, and rotten scree in late-season/low-snow conditions (not a place to slip — a fall could be hard to arrest given the loose surface), while a lingering snowfield/snow-finger makes for a faster, more secure glissade-and-plunge-step descent earlier in the season. Stay well clear of Gilhooley Tower's east/direct side on the way down, as steep ground there has been the site of serious injuries; the safe line goes around to the west as on the ascent. From Upper Royal Basin, retrace the approach: back down past Shelter Rock to Royal Lake, then out FST 832/FST 833 to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Bring 2-3 ice screws or snow pickets for emergency anchor points. Most climbers bring lightweight rope (30-50m) for emergency situations though standard route does not require roped climbing.
rack: 2-3 ice screws or snow pickets (emergency anchor points, glacier crossing)
30-50m rope (optional, emergency use — standard route does not require roped climbing)
current.pro_needs: Largely an unroped scramble; parties may want a rope and minimal gear for protecting or belaying short exposed steps depending on conditions and comfort.
current.rope_note: Royal Basin approach crosses the top edge of a small glacier where crevasse danger is described as minimal; remainder is Class 2 loose scree/pillow lava. Steep, exposed and serious, primarily due to rockfall risk, not technical difficulty — helmet essential, rope not standard.

name: East Route / Standard
beta: This is the peak's normal route and the line most parties use, climbed via the Despair Lakes basin and the southeast face. Terrain ranges from 3rd-class scrambling on the lower face to short sections of low-5th-class rock (to about 5.0) on the final summit block, including a vertical dihedral typically protected and climbed with a half-length rope. The bigger challenge is the approach itself: a long, remote, largely off-trail traverse over two passes with real route-finding difficulty and brush.
overview: Mount Despair is a remote, twin-summited granite peak in the North Unit of North Cascades National Park, its glaciated cirques draining north into Bacon Creek and south into Goodell Creek. Named by USFS surveyor Lage Wernstedt in the 1920s (the name first appeared on Forest Service maps in 1931), it saw its first ascent in 1939 by a 16-year-old Fred Beckey and two companions. The peak sits in the same remote, trail-less cluster as Mount Triumph, Mount Terror, and Bacon Peak, and is known among North Cascades climbers less for technical difficulty on the summit block than for its long, brushy, multi-day approach via Thornton Lakes and Triumph Pass.

current.approach: Start at the Thornton Lakes Trailhead (~2,500 ft), reached via the rough spur road off SR-20 near milepost 117. Follow the Thornton Lakes Trail/old roadbed on a nearly flat first mile to a crossing of Thornton Creek — the last reliable, easy water source before the route goes fully off-trail. From the creek, leave the maintained tread and begin bushwhacking up-slope: expect a series of small cliff bands that force a leftward (northerly) traverse through thickets of slide alder, then a ferny talus slope above a 3,800-ft hanging meadow, followed by a steep, brushy push of about 1,000 ft through cedar limbs and heavy brush to a rocky shoulder at roughly 5,300 ft on Thornton Ridge. Budget most of a day for this stretch alone (parties have taken 7+ hours from trailhead to the shoulder) — it is the crux of the approach in terms of effort and route-finding, not the climbing itself. From the Thornton Ridge shoulder, traverse north over rock and heather, working around minor terrain obstacles, to flat benches near 6,050-ft Thornton Pass — the standard camp for this route (most parties treat this as a 2-3 day trip rather than a car-to-car push). From camp, descend back to about 5,300 ft and cross roughly 1.5 hours of shoulder-high brush to a cascading stream with open bedrock slabs (a second water source); down-climb the slabs about 200 ft, then drop through forest and steep duff for another 500 ft to about 4,600 ft. Traverse into the open basin below Triumph Pass and climb to the 5,500-ft pass. From Triumph Pass, descend a north-facing snowfield to about 4,900 ft, skirt Lake Regret (often partly frozen) on its west-side moraine, then re-climb to roughly 5,300 ft and traverse several miles of heather benches, slabs, and shallow ravines to 5,100-ft Upper Despair Lake. From the lake, climb a heathery ridge to the east, then talus and snow, to reach the cliff band directly below Despair's southeast face/east ridge, where the technical climbing begins. Total approach mileage/gain to this point is substantial — trip reports covering the full round trip (trailhead to summit and back) log roughly 24 miles and 12,000+ ft of cumulative gain and loss, consistent with this route's recorded ~38.6 km distance. Key hazards: creek crossing at Thornton Creek (usually a rock-hop, can be pushier in early season snowmelt); loose, vegetated rock in the cliff bands above Thornton Creek; extended off-trail travel with real route-finding consequences (parties have gotten cliffed out and had to backtrack); and lingering snow patches/steep snow chutes near Despair Lakes into early summer.
approach_variant_names: Thornton Lakes, Thornton Pass and Triumph Pass to the Despair Lakes basin
current.descent: The 'standard'/East Route descent reverses the east ridge on which most modern parties actually climb (rather than the steeper southeast-face dihedral line some early parties used). This is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route: parties who instead climbed the SE-face dihedral variant found they had to rappel that single pitch to get back onto the ridge, then realized the East Ridge itself offers an easy, continuous Class 3 downclimb that avoids rope work entirely — this is why it's now treated as the standard descent. From the summit, downclimb the east ridge (Class 3, exposed but not technical) back to the cliff band above Upper Despair Lake; if that band is wet or a party prefers not to downclimb it, a single short rappel (roughly a half rope-length, natural gear/sling anchor off a horn or block — no fixed/bolted anchors are reported on this remote route) is a reasonable fallback, but it is not required under normal dry conditions. From the cliff band, reverse the approach: back down to Upper Despair Lake, across the multi-mile heather/slab/ravine traverse to the Lake Regret moraine, up and over the north-facing snowfield to Triumph Pass, down into the basin, back up the steep duff/slab down-climb section to about 5,300 ft, over Thornton Ridge, and down through the brush and cliff bands to Thornton Creek and the trailhead. Parties doing this in a single push from camp report full days (12+ hours) with the final stretch through talus and brush often finishing in the dark — bring headlamps and expect the descent to take as long as or longer than the ascent given the sustained off-trail terrain. No fixed rappel stations exist on this route; any rope use is opportunistic (natural anchors) rather than an established rappel line.
current.detailed_rack: Light rack of cams and slings for the exposed summit blocks; most of the route is unroped scrambling.
current.pro_needs: Class 4 scrambling with short exposed steps; a light rack and rope handle the crux and summit moves.

name: Northeast Buttress ("Bipolar Buttress")
beta: The route climbs the northeast buttress of Mt. Despair's north summit, starting low in the green, rugged Goodell Creek valley. It opens with roughly 1,300 ft of 5.6 climbing up an open-book corner on the lower buttress, followed by scenic but progressively technical scrambling over a series of notches that require short rappels to pass. The crux is a deep cleft (several hundred feet) near the top of the upper buttress; the first-ascent party found a 70m, 5.9 pitch up a right-trending ramp through it after judging the opposite wall too steep, loose, and hard to access. A shorter technical pitch and more moderate climbing follow, then a final 70m steep rock pitch gains the upper north ridge, which is followed via a snow ridge to the summit. It is technically rewarding, but the good climbing is reached only through serious effort over rough, unpleasant ground.
overview: A ~3,700 ft previously-unclimbed buttress line up Mt. Despair's northeast side to its north summit, opened in 2014: an easy 5.6 opening corner, a series of notches requiring short rappels, a stout 5.9 pitch through a deep summit-area cleft, a further steep pitch to the north ridge, and a snow-ridge finish.

current.approach: Approach is up a brush-choked valley low in the Goodell Creek drainage — rough enough that even seasoned Cascades climbers have balked at it. This is the opposite (northeast) side of the peak from the standard Triumph Pass/Despair Lakes approach.
current.descent: From the north summit, the first-ascent party exited over Triumph Pass and out the Thornton Lakes Trail rather than retracing the Goodell Creek approach.
current.detailed_rack: A rock rack sufficient for sustained 5.6 and a 5.9 crux pitch (small to mid-size cams and nuts), a 70m rope, plus extra slings/cord for building rappel anchors at the intermediate notches.
current.pro_needs: Gear is needed most for the sustained lower corner (5.6) and the crux 70m ramp pitch (5.9) through the deep cleft; natural anchors (horns, gear placements) back up the several short rappels over intermediate notches.

name: Standard Trail (Upper Trailhead, NFR 24)
beta: From the upper trailhead the trail climbs almost immediately via stacked switchbacks for about 0.3 mile before merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. From there it continues at a steady, 'character-building' grade through forest, breaks out of the trees into rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows, passes through a notch, and finishes with a short scramble to the true summit. It is a non-technical trail/scramble (no rope or rack needed in summer conditions) but is consistently steep with minimal flat ground. This is the standard, most direct route; a longer alternative starts from the lower trailhead (2,600 ft, no fee) and joins the same trail at the 3,900 ft merge point.
overview: Mount Ellinor (5,944 ft) is one of the most popular and heavily trafficked summits in the southeastern Olympics, on Trail #812 in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness of Olympic National Forest, rising directly above Lake Cushman. The trail climbs through old-growth forest into open subalpine parkland to a narrow summit ridge with sweeping views of Lake Cushman, Hood Canal, the Kitsap Peninsula, and — on clear days — Mount Rainier and neighboring Mount Washington and The Brothers. The mountain is best known regionally for its long, sun-exposed spring snow chute, one of the most reliable early-season glissades in the Olympics, and for the crowds it draws on summer weekends given its short approach relative to the payoff.

current.approach: From the Upper Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24/FS 2419 — the lot has a vault toilet, picnic table, and requires a Northwest Forest Pass), Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is a set of stacked, stairstep switchbacks gaining steadily through forest before the upper-trailhead route merges with the longer lower-trailhead trail (2,600 ft TH, 3.1 mi one-way) at roughly 3,900 ft. From the junction, continue up along the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline (~4,500 ft) around 1 mile in. Here is a well-signed junction where the winter/climbers' route breaks right up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, while the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, many switchbacks having stairstep risers that add to the grade. In summer conditions (roughly July–October) the trail is snow-free and well-cut essentially to the top, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes before the final approach to the 5,944 ft summit — total gain from the Upper TH is 2,444 ft over 1.6 mi one-way. There is no reliable water source on the upper route; carry all the water you need. Outside of core summer (roughly November–June), snow typically fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties climb the chute directly instead of the buried summer trail — this demands an ice axe and traction devices (crampons/microspikes), and the terrain is a steep, funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check avalanche conditions before heading up, and note that rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside of full winter conditions.
approach_variant_names: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail
The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
current.descent: Descend Trail #812 back to the Upper Trailhead — this is a hike/scramble with a walk-down descent and no rappelling on the standard route (0 rappels, no technical anchors involved). When the upper mountain still holds a firm, continuous snowpack in the chute (common well into early summer most years), the popular and much faster descent line leaves the summer switchbacks and drops directly down the chute below the summit saddle: with an ice axe carried in self-arrest position, this is a well-known glissade losing roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes, with glissaders reportedly hitting 10+ mph on good snow. This is genuinely consequential terrain, not a casual slide — an uncontrolled or involuntary glissade, a fall on hard/icy snow without self-arrest skill, or exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute can cause serious injury, so only glissade in full control and bail to the trail if conditions look icy, rocky, or overly fast. Later in the season, as snow in the chute thins and exposes talus and rock, glissading becomes dangerous rather than fun, and the correct call is to stay on the maintained summer switchbacks for the entire descent. Whichever line is taken above timberline, the two rejoin at the signed timberline junction around 4,500 ft. The next junction below that, at roughly 3,900 ft, is a different one and works the other way: it is where the longer lower-trailhead trail splits off, and it is the recorded spot where parties descend to the wrong trailhead, so stay on the upper-trailhead branch there unless you deliberately left a shuttle car at the lower lot. From that merge it is a straightforward 0.3-mile drop down the stacked switchbacks back to the Upper Trailhead parking area.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection needed.
current.rope_note: Standard summer route from the Upper Trailhead is a hike/scramble that does not typically require rope or ice axe. Winter/early-season conditions require ice axe and crampons for a steep snow chute to the summit.

name: Standard Route
beta: Mount Fairchild is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range and is accessed via two primary routes: (1) the High Divide approach via Sol Duc and Mount Carrie, or (2) from the Elwha River over Mount Fitzhenry. Both routes involve significant glacier travel with crevasse hazards and require proper alpine mountaineering skills. The peak stands at the head of Fairchild Creek with the Fairchild Glacier on its east slope.
overview: Mount Fairchild (6,899 ft) is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range, a glaciated subrange deep in the interior of Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It carries the small, retreating Fairchild Glacier on its northeast flank and sits about 0.84 mi northeast of higher neighbor Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). No trail comes anywhere close to the summit — nearly all ascents are made as a side-trip during the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone climb, and the peak sees only a handful of ascents most years. First climbed in 1963 by Denny Pruitt, Dan Baker, Jack Christiansen, and Roy Etten.

current.approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel. In late July the glacier east of Mount Carrie can be skirted along its northwest edge on rock; drop to a tarn near 5,900 ft, hold that height to a gully that rises straight to the ridge, then walk the ridge to the top.
approach_variant_names: High Divide and Cat Basin to the Fairchild Glacier
current.descent: This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, descend the Southwest Ridge, circle back around the north side of the peak and reclimb the Carrie Glacier roped up with crampons to Mount Carrie's summit, then descend Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill back across Carrie's south face (or take the north-side alternative), then recross the Catwalk to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit for the Fairchild Glacier crossing; light gear for Class 2-3 rock
current.pro_needs: Glacier protection where snow/ice is present; minimal rock pro
bivy: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground

name: Southeast Face / Leroy Basin
beta: The standard route follows the Phelps Creek Trail to Leroy Basin, then goes cross-country north across a ridge saddle, descends roughly 700-1,000 ft to cross a small glacier/snowfield beneath Fernow's north/east side (informally called Gloomy Glacier), then climbs loose gullies and ridge terrain to a saddle south of the summit before a short, exposed scramble to the top. It is generally rated Class 3-4 with brief class 5 moves reported near the summit, and is one of the longer, more remote scrambles among Washington's highest peaks. Alternate approaches exist via the Entiat River/Cottonwood trailhead (less avalanche exposure, favored in winter) and via the Holden Village ferry and Copper Creek/east ridge.
overview: Mount Fernow (9,249 ft) is the 8th-highest peak in Washington and the state's third-highest non-volcanic summit, capping the Entiat Mountains sub-range of the North Cascades within the Glacier Peak Wilderness, Chelan County. The headwaters of the Entiat River rise from its south slopes. It was first climbed in 1932 by Oscar Pennington and Hermann Ulrichs, and named by USFS supervisor Albert H. Sylvester for Bernhard Fernow, a pioneering 19th-century American forester. Fernow sits close to Seven Fingered Jack and Mount Maude, and the three are commonly linked into one trip from a shared Leroy Basin camp (locally nicknamed the 'Entiat 9ers'). The standard line climbs the broad south-facing terrain above Leroy Basin — called both the 'Southeast Face' and the 'Southwest Slope' — culminating in an exposed, loose summit block.

current.approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, at the end of the Phelps Creek spur off Chiwawa River Road/FR-62), follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the valley. The tread is in generally good maintained shape, with only occasional overgrown brush in late summer. At about 3.5 miles (roughly 1.5-2 hours in), the trail runs alongside Leroy Creek — a large waterfall visible up-valley from the switchbacks is a good landmark — where an unsigned but well-beaten climbers' path breaks off on the north (true right) side of the creek. This use trail is unmaintained but easy to follow from steady foot traffic; it climbs very steeply, gaining roughly 2,000 ft in about 1.5-1.9 miles while staying above Leroy Creek, which is the last reliable water before the basin. It eases into Leroy Creek Basin (~6,050-6,100 ft, about 5.4 mi and ~2,700 ft gain from the trailhead), a broad heather-and-boulder cirque that is the standard base camp, with good tent sites and running water. From camp most parties continue north/northeast across meadow and rock toward a col (~7,800 ft) on Seven Fingered Jack's south shoulder, roughly another hour. This whole upper section is cross-country with sparse cairns — Fernow itself isn't visible from most of Leroy Basin, and the peak has a well-earned reputation for tricky route-finding, so carry a map/GPS track rather than counting on a visible target. From the col, the route loses about 1,000 ft into the basin below the Gloomy Glacier, crossing beneath a shrinking glacier remnant (open crevasses have been reported here — rope up for the crossing or give it a wide berth), then climbs the broad talus/scree slopes below Fernow's summit, roughly a mile toward the summit block, mostly class 2-3 talus with one notably exposed 'unexpected crux' — a sloped, gravel-covered slab with about a 30 m drop below and a 10 m traverse across it, rated only class 2 but consequential.
approach_variant_names: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
Holden Village and Copper Basin
Entiat River from Cottonwood
current.descent: Descend the same line used on ascent — Fernow's summit sits atop a maze of loose gullies and there is no reliable shortcut. From the top, downclimb the class 4 (occasionally low 5th, but the harder moves can be sidestepped) summit block; some parties, especially in wet rock or with a less experienced group, sling a horn or block on the north side of the block for a quick single rappel instead of downclimbing the crux moves — there are no fixed or bolted anchors on this route, so bring a couple of slings/rap rings to build a natural anchor, and a 30 m rope is sufficient (it's used to protect just the short crux section, not to reach the ground, so most parties still downclimb the remainder). Below the block, retrace the choss gully to about 8,800 ft, re-cross the exposed sloped-slab traverse with care (more consequential descending than ascending), then continue down the talus/scree valley back toward the glacier remnant, watching again for the crevasse near the plateau. From there you must reclimb roughly 1,000 ft back up to the Seven Fingered Jack col before dropping into Leroy Basin; an alternate some parties use off the col instead drops climber's-right across sandy ledges and down through large boulders directly to the basin, trading the reclimb for its own loose, ankle-twisting terrain. The descent is worse underfoot than the climb up — expect a great deal of loose rock, near-misses, and slips — so wear a helmet the whole way and plan to be off the summit block and crux traverse before dark. From Leroy Basin, reverse the steep climbers' trail back down to Phelps Creek Trail #1511 and out to the trailhead. Because the round trip from Leroy Basin alone can run 10-13+ hours, most parties treat the climb as a 2-3 day trip, camping at Leroy Basin going in and out rather than pushing car-to-car in a day.
current.detailed_rack: Many parties carry a short rope (30-60m) with a light rack of slings and a few small pieces of protection for the brief class 4-5 exposed moves near the summit block; a picket or two is useful for firm snow on the glacier/snowfield traverse below the ridge, especially early season.
rack: 30-60m rope (optional, for the exposed Class 4-5 summit moves)
A few small cams or nuts
1-2 snow pickets (glacier/snowfield traverse below the ridge)
current.pro_needs: Mostly natural/scrambling protection; a small rack of slings and a few small cams or nuts cover the short exposed class 4-5 section near the top. Snow pickets are more useful than rock gear for most parties, for the glacier/snowfield crossing below the ridge.
current.rope_note: Most of this is unroped scrambling, but carry a 30 m rope and a light rack of slings with a few small cams or nuts for the summit block: the last moves are exposed Class 4 with brief Class 5 reported. There are no fixed or bolted anchors anywhere on the route, so if you rappel the crux rather than downclimb it - which parties do on wet rock or with a less experienced group - you build the anchor yourself off a slung horn, and a couple of rap rings are worth the weight. A 30 m is enough because it protects that short section rather than reaching the ground. Add an ice axe and a picket or two for the remnant glacier and snowfield traverse below the ridge, and a helmet for the loose gullies.

name: South Slopes (Bailey Range)
beta: No maintained trail reaches Mount Ferry. The peak's easiest line is rated class 2 hiking and is approached entirely off-trail, staged from a camp at Ferry Basin (also called Ferry Glacial Lake or Ice Lake) in the cirque of the now-vanished Ferry Glacier. Nearly all ascents happen mid-traverse on the classic Bailey Range Traverse, a remote, mostly-unmarked alpine route connecting the Sol Duc and Elwha drainages.
overview: Mount Ferry (6,195 ft) is the eighth-highest peak in the Bailey Range, rising above the glacial tarns of Ferry Basin between Stephen Peak (2.3 mi NW) and Mount Pulitzer (0.6 mi SW, its nearest higher neighbor). Named by the 1889-90 Seattle Press Expedition for Governor Elisha P. Ferry. It is almost never climbed as a standalone objective -- nearly every ascent is a side-summit tagged mid-trip during the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse, the off-trail alpine high route linking Sol Duc's High Divide to the Elwha valley. The summit block itself is a straightforward walk-up over loose 'Olympics dagger' scree from Ferry Basin; the real difficulty of this route is the days of off-trail travel, routefinding, and exposed ridge traverses required just to reach its base.

current.approach: There is no dedicated trailhead, road, or maintained path to Mount Ferry — reaching it means committing to 2-3 days of the Bailey Range Traverse, Olympic National Park's classic off-trail high route that links the Sol Duc River trailhead (via Sol Duc Falls Trail #630) in the north with the Elwha River/Whiskey Bend trailhead in the south, or with the North Fork Quinault trailhead via Dodwell-Rixon Pass on the longer loop variant. The most common approach starts at the Sol Duc Trailhead: maintained trail runs about 1 mile to Sol Duc Falls, then climbs steadily past Deer Lake and up the High Divide Trail toward Bogachiel Peak/Heart Lake — roughly 9-11 miles and ~3,300 ft of gain from the car, and the last reliable on-trail water and camp before travel goes off-trail. From High Divide near Cat Basin, the route leaves the maintained trail and follows the Bailey Range crest east: over Cat Peak's exposed 'Catwalk' (an airy class 3 knife-edge ridge, the first of two such sections on the traverse) and Stephen Peak, where steep heather benches with class 3-4 moves lead into a second, brushier catwalk with awkward gully crossings serious enough to warrant a blunt 'don't. Fall.' warning before dropping into Ferry Basin (~5,700 ft), the standard camp beneath Mount Ferry and roughly 2 days / 15-20 miles of travel in. Ferry Basin has dependable water — a small waterfall about 60 ft from the usual camp spot, plus a nearby tarn — and is often considered one of the nicer camps on the traverse. From camp, Ferry's summit is reached via a broad bench and scree/talus slope east of the true summit, loose 'dagger scree' (sharp, shifting shale-like rock) that demands careful footing but involves no technical climbing, just sustained off-trail scrambling. A less-common southern approach comes in via Dodwell-Rixon Pass and Queets Basin, up Ball Bearing Gully to the Scott-Ludden saddle, then along the Ferry-Ludden ridge to that same broad bench east of the summit. Either way, expect no signage, no bridges, unmarked creek fords, lingering snow/ice in gullies and on north-facing slopes even in August (ice axe and often crampons are standard kit), slide alder brush lower on the flanks, and serious route-finding responsibility — this is remote, high alpine terrain well beyond the maintained trail network.
approach_variant_names: Bailey Range crest to Ferry Basin
current.descent: Mount Ferry has no rappels and no technical descent — it is a scramble summit reached and left entirely on foot, so treat rappels as 0. The standard way down reverses the ascent scree/talus slope on the peak's southeast side, which parties describe as distinctly easier than the way up — practically a stroll on milder, more consolidated ground compared to the loose dagger scree above Ferry Basin — dropping back onto the broad bench and rejoining the Bailey Range crest route. From there, parties continuing the traverse typically down-climb roughly 200 ft through a small connecting canyon southwest to the Ferry-Pulitzer saddle to press on toward Mount Pulitzer and eventually Bear Pass, while parties treating Ferry as an out-and-back reverse the route back to Ferry Basin camp and retrace the catwalks over Stephen and Cat Peaks to High Divide and the Sol Duc Trailhead. Parties continuing the full traverse southward instead drop via Dodwell-Rixon Pass into Queets Basin and the Elwha headwaters, eventually exiting via the Elwha Snowfinger — historically a reliable permanent snowfield but now reportedly in shambles, requiring steep, slippery side-hilling on grass and talus above the canyon plus stream crossings rather than a straightforward snow glissade; this exit is consistently rated among the hardest days of the traverse. Whichever way you leave Ferry, expect the same hazards as the approach in reverse: loose scree, exposed class 3-4 moves on the catwalks, lingering snow/ice in shaded gullies, and multi-day off-trail route-finding with no cell coverage until you rejoin High Divide or a trailhead road.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock or ice gear is needed for the South Slopes line itself. Parties commonly carry a lightweight glacier kit (thin rope, slings, a picket or two) for other glacier crossings elsewhere on the Bailey Range Traverse; ice screws are generally unnecessary.
current.rope_note: South Slopes descent/ascent is described in trip reports as easy scree ('practically a stroll') compared to the Southeast Ridge ascent line. No rope or rack needed.

name: South Face / Southeast Ledges
beta: Starting from Spider-Formidable Col (7,380 ft), this route descends east then contours across the south and southeast faces via a system of ledges and slabs. Multiple gullies offer access; climbers must identify the correct gully system to summit as other lines lead to false summits or dead ends. The route involves steep, exposed fourth and low fifth-class scrambling with loose rock throughout, typically requiring a rope and protection. This is the primary summit route and only practical descent.
overview: Mount Formidable is a prominent, aptly named peak on the classic high route between Cascade Pass and Dome Peak (the Ptarmigan Traverse). Herman Ulrichs named it in 1935 for the rugged appearance of its north face; it was first climbed via this general line on July 25, 1938 by Calder Bressler, Ray Clough, Bill Cox, and Tom Myers of the Ptarmigan Climbing Club during their pioneering 13-day traverse of the North Cascades. Despite its modest Class 3-4 rating, the South Face/Southeast Ledges route has a reputation among North Cascades climbers as deceptively serious: the correct summit gully is genuinely hard to pick out of several look-alike options, the rock is loose gneiss throughout, and a party member died in a fall while crossing the exposed rib/chasm below the true summit in August 2006.

current.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — a well-graded trail, roughly 1.5-2 hours at a steady pace. This is the last maintained tread; everything beyond is boot-path/climbers'-trail, the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse. From the pass, leave the trail and climb/contour east and north below Cache Ridge toward Cache Col (~6,903 ft), crossing the toe of the Cache Glacier — generally a mellow, low-crevasse-hazard crossing in early/mid season but rope up if it's opened out or snow-covered, since crevasse hazard has caught parties off guard here in low-snow years. From Cache Col, descend a talus traverse on a good climbers' trail down to Kool-Aid Lake (6,100 ft), a small meltwater tarn that is the standard base camp for the route (no permit required, no fires) — roughly 3 hours and 5-6 miles from Cascade Pass, so plan on 5-7 hours trailhead-to-camp overall. From Kool-Aid Lake continue south past Art's Knoll to the broad, well-known 'Red Ledge' — an exposed traverse over loose rock and (often) lingering snow patches that many parties choose to rope for; it is the most consistently reported crux of the approach and is noticeably worse when snow-covered. Beyond Red Ledge, follow a rough climbers' path roughly a mile over meadows, snow, talus, and small rock ribs toward the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall (~6,500 ft), then rope up and ascend the glacier's left/SSE side, weaving through crevasses, to the Spider-Formidable col (7,320 ft). From the col, descend/traverse (plunge-stepping snow, crampons for icy sections) to a flat camp/staging area below the south face snow slope near a notch around 7,050 ft — this is the jump-off point for the climb proper. From there the final approach to the route gains the south-face snowfield alcove via one of two options: a hidden gully on the left (reportedly with 5th-class moves) or, more commonly, a winding ledge on the right rated 3rd class with one 3rd-class-plus section. Water is available at Kool-Aid Lake and from glacier meltwater streams along the Middle Cascade Glacier margins; carry enough for the long, exposed traverse sections beyond. Overall this is a long, remote glacier-and-ledge approach with real route-finding demands — most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with camp at Kool-Aid Lake or the south-face notch rather than a single push.
approach_variant_names: Cascade Pass and the Ptarmigan Traverse to the Spider-Formidable col
current.descent: The standard descent reverses the ascent line rather than following a separate walk-off. From the summit, downclimb the cairned class-3 summit gully back to the ledge system, then reverse the exposed, loose class 3/3+ ledge traverse above the chasm back to the snowfield alcove — parties commonly keep the rope on and simul-climb this section for protection, especially with any snow on the ledges. Where the ledge/gully sections are snow-covered, icy, or judged too exposed to downclimb safely, parties rappel rather than reverse the moves on foot: parties describe two short rappels (roughly 30-60 ft each) off natural anchors — slung boulders/chockstones backed up with cordelette, occasionally an overhanging rappel off a slung boulder to reach mellow snow below — getting parties back down to the snowfield/notch area. There are no bolted or fixed anchors on this route; anchors are built from gear you carry (cordelette, slings) around horns and boulders, and the last person down typically retrieves what can be retrieved, though some parties report leaving a sling or cordelette behind. A single 30m rope is generally sufficient for these short raps, but carry extra cord/webbing since natural anchors here are ad hoc. From the notch/camp area, reverse the full approach: re-cross the Middle Cascade Glacier to the Spider-Formidable col, traverse back over Red Ledge, return to Kool-Aid Lake, climb back over Cache Col and the Cache Glacier, and descend the Cascade Pass Trail to the trailhead. Because this reversal is long, start the descent with enough daylight — at least one party describes finishing the ledge traverse back to camp by headlamp after a late summit. A minority of parties have explored an alternate exploratory descent from the south-face camp down Drop Creek to the South Fork Cascade River and an old, unmaintained gauging-station trail/road, but this involves a technical box-canyon traverse with roped tree-belays through steep brush and is not a recommended standard line — treat it as an emergency/exploratory option only. Key descent hazards: loose rock on the ledge/gully downclimb (worse when wet or snow-covered), rockfall risk while building rappel anchors or below parties above, reopening crevasses on the glacier crossings in the afternoon warmth (favor an early start/return), and the general seriousness of a long, complex reversal in a remote basin.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack of cams and nuts to two inches handles the brief fifth-class climbing.
current.pro_needs: Light; protection mainly for the upper rock steps.
bivy: Ridge benches above Yang Yang Lakes

name: North Buttress
beta: The route rises straight out of Luna Cirque above Lousy Lake on the north side of Fury, starting from around 5,600 ft near the cirque floor. Begin on steep snow, then work into a couloir system - a bergschrund at the base often forces a rock bypass, and in late season that bypass has been reported as dirty 5.6 - and follow it toward the buttress crest, crossing snowfields exposed to rockfall from hanging glaciers above. Higher up, snow, rock and moats alternate and the route-finding is tricky, with protection not always where you want it; near the crest a slabby step of about 5.9 is the technical crux, after which an airy but easier traverse around the right side of the ridge leads to a snow arete running to the summit. One party reached the ridge crest in about 4.5 hours from a camp at 4,000 ft in Luna Cirque. Alan Kearney, who repeated it in September 1992 with Mark Price, noted that the late season made for much more rock climbing down low, since Beckey and Davis in July 1962 climbed a lot of snow and avoided most of the rock.
overview: A Beckey classic and one of the great long alpine lines of the Pickets: roughly 4,000 ft and about 20 pitches of mixed snow and rock rising out of Luna Cirque to East Fury's summit, mostly Class 3, 4 and low 5th with a single 5.9 crux and a snow arete finish.

current.approach: Two very different ways in, both serious. The usual modern approach mirrors the Luna Col approach and then drops over the back: SR 20 to the Ross Dam trailhead, a mile of trail to the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, the Ross Lake Resort boat to Big Beaver Landing at about 1,600 ft, then 10-11.5 miles of Big Beaver Creek Trail past 39 Mile Camp to Luna Camp, another mile or so to the marked cut-off, a log crossing of Big Beaver Creek just north of Access Creek, and the Access Creek bushwhack (north bank through huckleberry, cross to the south bank near 3,800 ft where the brush pinches out) to Access Creek Basin at 4,300 ft. From there the scree chute to Access Col at 6,100 ft and the steep heather traverse to Luna Col at about 7,100-7,200 ft. From Luna Col descend north-northwest into Luna Cirque to Luna Lake at about 4,800 ft and continue southwest to a camp on the cirque floor beneath the buttress. The whole approach runs about 17 miles and 7,000 ft of gain from the Ross Lake water-taxi dock, and the descent from Luna Col into the cirque costs another 2,400 ft that has to be regained on the way out. Alan Kearney's party came in from the north instead, from Chilliwack Lake in Canada up the Chilliwack River Trail, over Whatcom Pass and across the Challenger Glacier before descending into Luna Cirque to camp at Luna Lake - a longer, higher and even more committing approach.
approach_variant_names: Luna Col, then over the back and 2,400 ft down into Luna Cirque to camp at Luna Lake
current.descent: The buttress is an ascent line only; the standard exit is over the top and down the other side. From the summit, downclimb the summit snowpatch (about 300 ft, 40 degrees at the base to nearly 50 degrees at the top - protect it with flukes or pickets, with the strongest climber first on belay) onto the Southeast Glacier, then descend the S-shaped snowfield past the bergschrund near 7,900 ft, keeping running belays where the gradient steepens and the runout is bad. Off the glacier, cross the rocky rib on the lower ledge, contour northeast through the talus basin, climb back up the heather chute to the northeast ridge crest, and follow the crest back over the terraced rock nose - one short rappel over the 25-ft step - to Luna Col. One traverse party instead descended the Southeast Glacier and continued toward Outrigger Peak and Picket Pass, which is the option if you are traversing the range rather than returning to Luna Col. Either way, a party that camped in Luna Cirque has to regain roughly 2,400 ft to Luna Col to retrieve gear and exit via Access Creek. Allow a full long day.
current.detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack plus snow gear. In short: a trad rack and a picket or two. In practice: a set of nuts, cams from small to about 2-3 inches, a few pitons are worth considering given the difficulty of finding solid placements, plenty of runners for wandering pitches, double ropes or a single 60 m plus a tag line for retreat, and one or two pickets.
current.pro_needs: Protection is the weak point of this route. Climbers report that route-finding is tricky and the protection is not always where you want it, so expect long runouts on Class 4 and low-5th ground and plan for a rack that lets you build belays quickly in imperfect rock. Snow protection matters as much as rock - a picket or two for the couloir and for the summit arete.

name: Southeast Glaciers (Standard)
beta: This is the standard approach to East Fury via Luna Peak traverse. The route is not technical climbing in the traditional sense but requires solid alpine skills, glacier travel proficiency, and exposure management on exposed scrambling. The terrain is predominantly Class 3–4 scrambling with one short Class 5.0 rock step (~25 feet, unroped passage is feasible). The glacier ascent is the crux: moderate 30–40 degree slopes steepen to 50+ degrees near summit with a large bergschrund requiring direct ascent. Route finding is straightforward following the ridge line and glacier, though descent via alternate terrain saves significant time over ascent route. Weather deterioration is the primary hazard—morning fog/clouds common at Luna Pass, clearing by midday.
overview: Mount Fury's East Peak is the standard-route summit of one of the most remote major peaks in the contiguous US, deep in North Cascades National Park's Northern Pickets. The Southeast Glacier route is technically moderate (Class 3-4 rock with a glaciated snow climb) but is guarded by one of the longest approaches in the Cascades — a full day of boat travel and trail hiking followed by two days of cross-country travel through brush, talus, and heather before the climbing even begins. Elevation surveys for East Fury range from the original 1953 USGS figure of 8,288 ft up to 8,356 ft in a 2022 theodolite survey, so treat any single number as approximate.

current.approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR 20 (~milepost 134, 2,150 ft), it's about 1 mile down to the Ross Lake water taxi dock; cross the lake by taxi (or paddle) to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail 11.5 miles up-valley — a dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail taking roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp around the 4.7-hour mark. About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp, a large (~15-inch-diameter) log crossing of Big Beaver Creek marks the turnoff: leave the trail here and head up the Access Creek drainage.
