This next mile is a real bushwhack, gaining roughly 1,900 ft (2,400 ft to 4,300 ft): start in valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then climb through moderately dense huckleberry brush before the final half-mile of talus into Access Basin — watch for deadfall, thick undercover, and biting insects. From Access Basin, a long, steep, loose scree chute gains ~1,800 ft to 6,100-ft Access Col (2-3 hours; can be brutally hot with no shade in the chute). From the col, traverse notoriously steep heather (an axe is worthwhile for security on the short, steep sections) and talus to Luna Pass, where most parties camp near lingering snow patches for water. From Luna Pass, skirt a rock knob that towers ~100 ft over the pass via a broad ledge on its northwest face to reach the surprisingly gentle Northeast Ridge crest, then follow the ridge's many short ups and downs — including a ~25-ft rock step with a climbable vertical crack (Class 3) — toward Fury. Where the ridge crest drops away, descend a steep, narrow heather chute (~500 ft) into a talus basin around 6,500 ft, then contour southwest across talus, heather, and polished slabs to a rocky rib that blocks easy passage; the lower of two ledge options (exposed scrambling on wet, mossy rock and steep heather) is generally preferred to the looser, more exposed upper ledge.
approach_variant_names: Ross Lake water taxi, Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col and Luna Pass
current.descent: This is fundamentally a walk-off/downclimb along the ascent line, not a rappel-heavy route, though one short technical step is often rappelled. From the summit, reverse the steep snowfield on a running belay with flukes (take particular care on the upper, firmer section — crampon-balling on wet snow has been reported), then retrace the Southeast Glacier descent, working back around the bergschrund. Regain the Northeast Ridge crest (parties often angle up sooner than the ascent line to save time) and reverse the rocky-rib traverse and heather-chute climb back to the ridge. At the ~25-ft rock step, many parties opt for a short single-pitch rappel rather than downclimbing the crack — a single 30m (or even shorter) rope is plenty, and the anchor is whatever natural gear (cams/nuts/slings on a horn or chockstone) the party builds, as there is no fixed/bolted station reported at this feature. From there, finish the ridge traverse back to Luna Pass. The following day, reverse the full approach: the heather/talus traverse and scree descent back to Access Col, the steep 1,800-ft drop into Access Basin, the Access Creek bushwhack (often taken as a more direct, steeper line straight down the brushy hillside rather than retracing the ascent line) back to the Big Beaver Creek log crossing, then the 11.5-mile Big Beaver Creek Trail out to the water taxi landing and back across Ross Lake to the Ross Dam Trailhead. One party took roughly 6 hours from the summit back to Luna Pass camp, and made the full round trip (camp to camp to trailhead) as a 4-day, ~42-mile, ~13,000 ft trip.
current.detailed_rack: Small, selective rock rack: 2–3 nuts (sizes #4–#6 Black Diamond or equivalent), 2–3 cams (sizes #0–#2 for the Class 5.0 crack step). Rock quality is variable (mix of good granodiorite and loose choss); expect poor protection and friable anchors. Primarily a protection rack for the single short technical step; most route management via scrambling and glacier travel.
rack: 25m rope for the short rappel descent (or full glacier rope)
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock climbing protection needed. The Class 5.0 rock step can be approached unroped by experienced alpinists. One 25-meter rope can be established for the short rappel descent. Glacier travel relies on snow anchor technology (flukes) rather than rock protection. Confidence on exposed Class 3–4 scrambling and efficient rope management required; this is an expedition-style climb.
current.rope_note: Standard route descends from Luna Col to the southeast glacier (~6,700ft), ascending its right side then steeper snow with a possible bergschrund crossing; snow/glacier terrain ranges 20-40 degrees, interspersed with Class 3-5 rock sections. A 30m rope per rope-team is typical, plus light rock protection for harder rock steps. Multi-day remote approach (allow ~1 week).

name: Northeast Buttress
beta: Grade III-IV alpine rock route with 5.4-5.5 climbing. Approach via 10-mile PCT descent to Bridge Creek junction, then 3-4 miles up North Fork Bridge Creek to base camp. Route ascends the Northeast Buttress with glacier travel, scrambling (3rd-4th class), and rock pitches up to 5.5. Total trip: 3-4 days recommended.
overview: The highest peak in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth country and a coveted Bulger summit, Mount Goode dominates the head of Bridge Creek. Its Northeast Buttress is a long, classic alpine rock climb on a grand mountain, pairing a glaciated approach with many pitches of moderate granite up a striking buttress.

current.approach: Southbound on the Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) down Bridge Creek, then northwest up North Fork Bridge Creek
approach_variant_names: Bridge Creek and the North Fork to the moat below the red ledges
current.descent: Descent is via the Southwest Couloir, downclimbed and rappelled from the summit ridge. The standard sequence is three rappels from the summit down along the ridge to Black Tooth Notch — the first rappel runs close to straight down the ridgeline, but the second and third are notably traversing (trending skier's right/rappeller's left), so there is real rope-snag risk and parties should watch their tails carefully. From the notch, simul-climb or scramble the connecting exposed 4th-class ledge, then make roughly three more single-rope rappels down into the SW couloir itself (six total is the commonly cited number, matching the route's historical rappel count; some parties link stations differently and report as few as five — e.g. two 30m rappels bridging the Black Tooth Notch section). A single 60m rope is sufficient for every station on this descent. Anchors are natural and fixed slings on horns/blocks rather than bolted stations, though they are described as 'well-established' — still, carry spare cord and rap rings to refresh sun-baked webbing. Below the raps, class 3 downclimbing continues down the couloir; where the gully narrows into cliffs lower down, exit left onto easier terrain and traverse back into the basin beneath the gully rather than rappelling the waterfall band. From the base of the couloir, descend scree/talus back to the Goode Glacier basin, re-cross the glacier, and reverse the approach down the North Fork Bridge Creek drainage to the PCT and trailhead — a long descent day that several parties report taking 8-10+ hours from summit to car, with real potential for benightment if the party is slow through the technical section.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from about #0.3 to #1 (some parties add a few small Aliens or C3 microcams, or double up 0.3-0.75, for long simul-climbing blocks), a set of nuts, and a few tricams -- useful for quick gear anchors on this mostly 3rd/4th-class buttress with short low-5th-class steps (5.5-5.7ish). Bring 8-14 alpine draws for the wandering, low-angle terrain, plus a handful of 60cm/120cm slings and a cordelette or double-length sling for anchors and a personal anchor system. No need for a heavy rack or doubled cams beyond the small-to-mid sizes.
current.pro_needs: Protection is intermittent -- most of the route is 3rd/4th-class scrambling with short low-5th-class steps, so gear placements are more about quick simul-climbing anchors than sustained crack climbing. A single light rack to about #1 plus a few tricams is standard; nobody needs a heavy or doubled rack.
current.rope_note: Rappels are 6 single-strand ~30m raps off the standard descent (3 summit-to-Black Tooth Notch, 3 into the SW Couloir) -- a single 60m rope is standard and sufficient. Do not bring a second rope; the "double rope" beta in older data appears to be a misreading of one party's skinny single-rated rope doubled over for simul-climbing protection, not two full ropes.
